title: Credential Signaling in Derivatives Markets
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Credential Signaling in Derivatives Markets

keywords: CFOA JEL Codes: D82 (Asymmetric and Private Information)

detail.abstract:
Global exchange-traded derivatives markets reached a record 180 billion contracts traded in 2024 (World Federation of Exchanges, 2025), yet the professional credential landscape governing those who operate within it remains dominated by broad-purpose designations that allocate only a marginal fraction of their curricula to derivatives-specific knowledge. Drawing on the canonical signaling framework developed by Spence (1973), this paper develops a theoretical account of why general financial credentials produce informationally weak signals in derivatives-specific hiring contexts, and why specialist credentials, those designed exclusively around futures, options, and structured instruments, generate superior separating equilibria in the labor market for derivatives professionals.

We argue that three structural features of exchange-traded derivatives markets, technical depth, margin dynamics, and tail-risk opacity, raise the employer’s cost of evaluating candidates using generalist signals alone, creating the conditions under which a specialist designation commands a meaningful informational premium. The paper applies this framework to assess the Certified Futures and Options Analyst (CFOA) designation as a market-rational response to this gap and discusses implications for hiring practices, risk governance, and credentialing policy more broadly.

detail.abstract: The ethical governance of AI in defence confronts a paradox: principles proliferate while implementation falters. This systematic review of 1,085 publications exposes why frameworks flounder where ethical governance matters most. We identify seven barriers—governance and structural, conceptual, strategic, operational, relational and cultural, technical and data, and resource constraints—that operate as an interconnected system. Governance and structural barriers dominate the literature. This prominence may reflect their visibility rather than their primacy; technical, operational, and cultural dynamics remain harder to trace but are equally consequential. The challenges created by these seven barriers are severe but not insurmountable. We propose three strategic interventions: establishing authoritative, interoperable governance architectures that transcend organisational and national boundaries; building institutional capacity through dedicated resources and interdisciplinary expertise; and integrating ethical governance as core capability throughout the AI lifecycle rather than as compliance retrofit. This systemic analysis advances scholarship beyond principle enumeration and towards understanding the institutional, structural, and technical conditions under which ethical governance of AI in the defence domain can acquire operational traction in contested strategic environments.

title: Empirical Asset Pricing via Learning-to-Rank
affiliations: University of Macau,  and Shenzhen University

detail.title: Empirical Asset Pricing via Learning-to-Rank
detail.abstract: We apply learning-to-rank to the cross-section of asset pricing. Unlike return forecast and probability forecast models that rank stocks based on their absolute values of return or probability forecasts, learning-to-rank models directly optimize relative rankings among stocks and rank stocks based on their relative orders. We show that learning-to-rank models outperform return and probability forecast models in terms of Sharpe ratios and maximum drawdowns. Combining return or probability forecasts with learning-to-rank does not consistently outperform learning-to-rank models alone. We apply the learning-to-rank philosophy to simpler models such as ordered logit models, which perform as well as the best sophisticated return and probability forecast machine learning models. Our results suggest that the learning-to-rank, a philosophy so far largely ignored in finance, sheds novel light on the cross-section of stock returns.

title: Factors Affecting Employee Engagement Under Work from Home (WFH) During the COVID-19 Pandemic: Empirical Evidence from a Selected Financial Company in Sri Lanka

detail.title: Factors Affecting Employee Engagement Under Work from Home (WFH) During the COVID-19 Pandemic: Empirical Evidence from a Selected Financial Company in Sri Lanka

declarations.ethicsApproval: Informed consent was obtained from all participants, and confidentiality was maintained. Formal ethics committee approval was not required.

detail.abstract: This study examines factors affecting employee engagement under work-from-home (WFH) arrangements during the COVID-19 pandemic, using evidence from a selected financial company in Sri Lanka. A quantitative, cross-sectional design was adopted, and data were collected from 214 employees using a structured questionnaire. Employee engagement was analyzed in relation to access to internet and IT devices, work–life balance, specified work plans, and sense of belonging. Correlation and multiple regression analyses reveal that access to internet and IT devices and sense of belonging have a significant positive impact on employee engagement, while work–life balance and specified work plans are not significant predictors.

title: When Human Narratives Meet Artificial Intelligence: Exploring a Framework for AI Ethics
affiliations: , Virginia Tech, University of Mississippi and

detail.title: When Human Narratives Meet Artificial Intelligence: Exploring a Framework for AI Ethics

declarations.funderStatement: This research was supported by the National Science Foundation under Award No. 2418867 (Collaborative Research: Mapping AI Ethics Education Through Intervention Types, Faculty Perceptions, and Institutional Contexts) and Award No. 2418848 (Collaborative Research: Incubation Project—Leveraging the Ethics Bowl Framework for Artificial Intelligence Ethics Education), both administered through the SBE Office of Multidisciplinary Activities at Virginia Tech.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping decision-making processes and infrastructures. It is also changing how societies narrate risk, responsibility, and the future. Existing scholarship has examined these representations and their ethical implications. Yet it rarely offers comprehensive approaches to analyzing the functions narratives perform in shaping ethical debates. Understanding these functions is crucial for grasping how narratives influence ethical judgment and public discourse about AI. To address this gap, this paper proposes a conceptual framework for examining them. Rather than analyzing narrative content or audience reception, we focus on narrative structure. We ask how these structures shape normative assumptions and guide ethical evaluation. We grounded the analysis in a qualitative integrative review. We developed a typology linking three narrative functions to three waves of ethical concern about AI. The framework offers a heuristic tool for analyzing how ethical discourse around AI is formed, contested, and transformed. More broadly, the paper promotes reflective, context-sensitive approaches to AI governance and public understanding. This is especially important today, as AI's disruption means that humans no longer shape narratives alone.

title: Gödel's Incompleteness and the Possibility of Immanent Philosophy: Spinoza, Wittgenstein, and the Strange Loop of Consciousness
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Gödel's Incompleteness and the Possibility of Immanent Philosophy: Spinoza, Wittgenstein, and the Strange Loop of Consciousness
detail.abstract: This paper examines whether Gödel's incompleteness theorems undermine the possibility of constructing an immanent philosophical system-one that is selfgrounding and requires no external foundation. Taking Spinoza's Ethics as the paradigmatic case, the paper distinguishes three levels at which the question can be posed: ontological immanence (Substance as causa sui), epistemic immanence (truth as self-certifying), and formal-syntactic self-grounding (the Ethics as a quasi-axiomatic text). Gödel's theorems directly constrain only the third of these, and by extension any finite reconstruction of the second; they say nothing directly about the first. The paper argues that this asymmetry, far from being a technicality, illuminates the structure of Spinoza's project. Drawing on Wittgenstein's metaphor of the ladder (Tractatus 6.54), it proposes that the Ethics functions as a transitional device-a formal system that succeeds by pointing beyond formalism toward scientia intuitiva, which by its nature cannot be captured propositionally. The convergence of a structurally similar insight across independent philosophical and contemplative traditions is noted as suggestive, though its evidential force depends on prior acceptance of Spinoza's parallelism. Finally, the paper offers a speculative hypothesis connecting Gödel's self-referential construction to the phenomenology of self-reflexive consciousness, proposing that the difficulty of the transition the traditions describe is rooted in the structural problem of a representational system attempting to transcend representation from within.

title: Measuring Values in Large Language Models
affiliations: Hebrew University of Jerusalem - Center for the Study of Rationality, The Hebrew University of Jerusalem - Business School, Hebrew University of Jerusalem, Hebrew University of Jerusalem - Hebrew University and Hebrew University of Jerusalem

detail.title: Measuring Values in Large Language Models
detail.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used as decision aids in contexts shaped by priorities rather than facts, yet their recommendations are often treated as objective. We show that a system of human values can be identified in LLMs and predicts outputs such as occupational and donation preferences. Across 11 models, we administered validated measures of values and preference tasks, finding parallels with humans in overall value priorities, the structure of value interrelations, and links between values and recommendations. Most models resembled human patterns, with variation across systems. When prompted to emphasize specific values, models displayed sharper tradeoffs and more value-consistent recommendations. These findings indicate that human–LLM parallels extend beyond surface attitudes to shared value structures, and that value theory captures core components useful for predicting model behavior.

title: Legitimacy by Design: Reframing Sustainability in Artificial Intelligence
affiliations: and

detail.title: Legitimacy by Design: Reframing Sustainability in Artificial Intelligence
detail.abstract: The ecological demands of Artificial Intelligence increasingly collide with what natural systems can support under current technological frontiers. The scale of this problem exceeds the reach of individual ethics. It calls instead for collective and institutional decision-making capable of sustaining technological legitimacy. This paper advances a framework for sustainable AI design that addresses this challenge. Grounded in the capability approach, the framework develops three anchors-AI as conversion factor, ecological stabilizer, and source of sufficiency. Each identifies a distinct way in which design can link technological development to the conditions that sustain human flourishing and environmental viability. Together, they offer normative criteria for evaluating whether AI contributes to desirable technological orders within existing material and institutional constraints. In doing so, we reframe sustainability-from an add-on design criterion to a principle of legitimate and just governance in technological development. Design decisions are not political acts in themselves. Still, they carry political weight. Understanding this helps make AI meet normative criteria for its social acceptance and legitimacy.

title: Corporation-Specific Anti-Takeover Statutes and the Market for Corporate Charters
affiliations: George Mason University - Antonin Scalia Law School

detail.title: Corporation-Specific Anti-Takeover Statutes and the Market for Corporate Charters

publicationDetails.detailsText: George Mason Legal Studies Research Paper
publicationDetails.journalName: Antonin Scalia Law School, George Mason University Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Most of the current corporate law literature contends that the competition among the states for corporate chartering business benefits shareholders because such competition allows managers to select the most suitable corporate law. The market for corporate control functions as an important corporate governance mechanism because the threat of takeover and removal of incumbent management provides an effective external source of discipline. The recent wave of takeover-specific antitakeover laws, however, has raised questions about the desirability of this competition. In this Article, Professor Henry Butler considers the connection between takeover- specific anti-takeover laws and the market for corporate control.

Professor Butler first analyzes the current array of anti-takeover devices. He concludes that a total prohibition of anti-takeover measures is not desirable but also believes that takeover-specific laws should be discouraged because their true purpose is to protect the jobs of incumbent management. Although these laws are the result of management misuse of corporate assets, Professor Butler finds the laws most objectionable because they create uncertainty for shareholders about the role of the market for corporate control in corporate governance.

Finally, Professor Butler examines how to prevent state legislatures from being used by managers who desire takeover-specific laws. He believes that some legislation is needed to remedy the problem of lack of notice to shareholders but finds the current decentralized patchwork of state laws preferable to the imposition of a potentially very costly and inefficient uniform federal law. Professor Butler concludes that the current takeover-specific anti-takeover laws are not the product of the market for corporate charters and suggests that the passage of takeover-specific laws will increase the value of incorporating in a state with stable and predictable corporate law.

title: Humanizing AI: How Anthropomorphic Chatbots Drive Customer Engagement in Online Travel Agencies
affiliations: Gurukul Kangri Vishwavidyalaya and Balaji Insistitute of Modern Management (BIMM)

detail.title: Humanizing AI: How Anthropomorphic Chatbots Drive Customer Engagement in Online Travel Agencies

publicationDetails.detailsText: International Journal of Tourism Research, volume 28, issue 2, 2026[10.1002/jtr.70285]

detail.abstract: This study investigates how AI anthropomorphism and perceived risk influence user trust and customer engagement in the hospitality and tourism industry, with a focus on Online Travel Agency (OTA) chatbots. Using survey data from 303 OTA users and structural equation modeling (SmartPLS 4.0), the research tests mediation by user trust and moderation by user experience. Findings show AI anthropomorphism significantly boosts trust and engagement, while perceived risk exerts no meaningful effect on trust and unexpectedly shows no direct negative influence on engagement. User trust does not directly drive engagement; however, when user experience is high, trust significantly enhances engagement. The study extends hospitality technology adoption theory by highlighting the indirect and conditional pathways linking anthropomorphic design to customer outcomes. Practical implications emphasize integrating subtle human‐like features and optimizing user experience to maximize engagement in AI‐powered OTA services.

title: The First Amendment and Federal Securities Regulation
affiliations: George Mason University - Antonin Scalia Law School

detail.title: The First Amendment and Federal Securities Regulation

detail.abstract:
A consideration of how the first amendment applies to federal securities regulation raises many fundamental normative and positive issues, such as the normative issue of whether it is desirable to use the First Amendment as a constraint on substantive economic regulation, and the positive issue of the relative costs and benefits of regulating speech. Clearly, the possibility of applying standard First Amendment analysis to federal securities regulation is intriguing.

To address some of these provocative issues, a symposium was held. The event was held at the then George Mason University School of Law, now Antonin Scalia Law School, in Arlington, Virginia on October 30 to November 2, 1986. This piece introduces the papers delivered at the conference.

title: The Art of Disagreement: Conflict Resolution in the Schools of Hillel and Shammai
affiliations: City University of New York (CUNY) - Koppelman School of Business and Yeshiva University

detail.title: The Art of Disagreement: Conflict Resolution in the Schools of Hillel and Shammai
detail.abstract: Knowing how to dispute constructively is vital in many areas of life, including law, society, economics, and business. We study the evolution of disputes by examining the Academies of Hillel and Shammai, two early Jewish schools of thought dominant in the latter half of the first century BCE. The disagreements and disputes between the two academies became quite intense and may even have resulted in physical clashes over voting on the law; the Shammaites thus threatened and restricted the voting of the Hillelites. It took a heavenly voice to declare that the law agrees with the School of Hillel. Interestingly, the voice also explained why the law follows the Hillel viewpoint: arguments are all well and good, but one must respect one's opponent. Their interactions over time have created a blueprint for constructive argumentation, even in our times.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence is reshaping the film and media industries across production, post-production, performance, rights management, distribution, and audience trust. This paper argues that AI should be analysed as an infrastructural transformation that reorganises transaction costs, labour bargaining power, contractual control, and informational asymmetries across the media value chain. Building on Schumpeter's theory of creative destruction, Coasean transaction-cost economics, and labour-monopsony theory, the paper proposes the General Theory of Creative Disruption+ (GTCD+). Within this framework, it introduces five analytical tools: the Risk-Adjusted Efficiency-Complexity Ratio (RA-ECR), the Transparency Asymmetry Principle, the Likeness Lock-In Risk (LLR), the Visibility Control Function (VCF), and the Authenticity and Trust Index (ATI). This is a conceptual and normative framework paper. These constructs are presented as illustrative heuristic instruments for analysing AI adoption. Future work is needed to calibrate and test them empirically in specific domains before they can support predictive or decision-oriented use. The paper situates them in relation to recent industry and regulatory developments, including AI-assisted screen production, disputes over training-data governance, synthetic-performer regulation, and audience disclosure expectations. It concludes with four policy recommendations for more sustainable integration of AI in film and media, including the proposed De Havilland Threshold for digital-likeness contracts.

detail.title: Pharmaceutical Pricing

declarations.declarationOfInterest: NA
declarations.ethicsApproval: NA
declarations.funderStatement: NA

detail.abstract: This chapter examines pharmaceutical pricing through a five-part framework: Cost, Customers, Channels, Competitors, and Compatibility. We synthesize how research and development (R&D) risk, patent and exclusivity rules, insurer design, healthcare providers, patients, and intermediaries including pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs), wholesalers, pharmacies, and group purchasing organizations (GPOs), jointly shape list and net prices. The chapter distinguishes small-molecule and biologic cost structures; explains how patents, generics, and biosimilars alter competitive conduct; and shows how formularies, cost-sharing, copay programs, and patient-assistance mechanisms reallocate spending. We also integrate recent policy interventions, including Medicare Part D reforms, transparency mandates, drug-importation rules, and the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) negotiation authority, and discuss their implications for innovation incentives and patient access. The chapter concludes with a forward-looking research agenda focused on developing innovative pricing models for high-cost therapies; examining global benchmarking and trade policies that influence R&D investment and affordability; assessing the effects of patient-assistance programs, copay coupons, and digital discount platforms; analyzing intermediary behavior and biosimilar competition within evolving market structures; and evaluating the impact of new U.S. pricing regulations through causal policy analysis.

title: Transforming First Impressions in Digital Marketing: Leveraging Artificial Intelligence to Transform Early-stage Consumer Engagement
affiliations: Arden University

detail.title: Transforming First Impressions in Digital Marketing: Leveraging Artificial Intelligence to Transform Early-stage Consumer Engagement
detail.abstract:
This dissertation presents a retrospective, current, and prospective analysis of the Artificial Intelligence impact on marketing, with an emphasis on early-stage consumer engagement. In an era marked by media saturation and diminishing consumer attention spans, brands face increasing pressure to establish meaningful engagement from the very first interaction. Artificial Intelligence has emerged as a transformative force in marketing, revolutionising data collection, segmentation, targeting, personalisation, and content creation. Despite exponential growth in AI research and adoption, academic literature has yet to fully address the strategic, operational, and ethical implications of AI in upper funnel marketing, especially regarding brand awareness, brand equity, and the privacy-personalisation paradox.

The study specifically focuses on three core areas: (1) the effectiveness of AI in optimising brand awareness and consideration, (2) the development of methodologies for monitoring AI’s impact on brand equity, and (3) the ethical balance between AI-driven personalisation and consumer privacy. The research aims to bridge the gap between academic theory and industry practice, offering actionable insights for both researchers and marketing professionals.

Employing a thematic analysis of secondary data, this study synthesises findings from 37 academic and 11 industry publications, filtered through systematic review protocols. Data sources include Google Scholar, Perplexity, Forbes, and McKinsey, ensuring a robust multi-perspective approach.

Key findings reveal that AI adoption in upper-funnel marketing significantly enhances brand awareness and consideration, outperforming traditional methods when paired with human oversight. AI-driven personalisation increases conversion rates. However, the privacy-personalisation paradox remains a critical challenge. The study recommends phased AI implementation, putting a human-centric strategy first, and the technology second. This study also recommends including new KPIs, such as Answer Share Rate and impressions from LLMs, to measure the impact of Artificial Intelligence on brand equity.

Limitations include reliance on short-term data collected through platforms owned by companies with a commercial interest in AI, as well as the underrepresentation of non-Western perspectives. Future research should address longitudinal impacts, cross-cultural consumers’ sensitivities, the evolving role of agentic AI in marketing, and the future of marketing organizations.

title: Talking without Speaking: Paid Trolls on Social Media and Court Decision
affiliations: Wisconsin School of Business and University of Minnesota - Twin Cities

detail.title: Talking without Speaking: Paid Trolls on Social Media and Court Decision
detail.abstract: With the massive growth of social media and other informational platforms that businesses and individuals may use to share their opinions, a society's perspectives of certain contentious issues may be influenced significantly. At the same time, it has been noted that various parties have used paid trolls (i.e., fake comments made by bot accounts) to sway public opinions concerning some hotly debated issues or legal proceedings. This article aims to investigate how public opinions and paid trolls may affect the outcome of legal disputes between opposing parties. Our research indicates that litigating parties involved in lawsuits with social media engagement may purchase paid trolls to influence public opinions, and they do so more significantly when the truth does not match the prior expectation of the public. We also discover that social media users' investigation may be a pitfall for the involved parties. Additionally, the court may be either constrained or aided to identify the truth by having a tendency to render decisions that align with prevailing public opinions, depending on the stake of the lawsuit. Finally, treating public opinions on social media as additional information that aids court decision may backfire.

title: TransUNet-Based Hybrid CNN–Transformer Architecture for Precise Plant Leaf Disease Segmentation and Classification
affiliations: Swami Ramanand Teerth Marathwada University and Shri Guru Gobind Singhji Institute of Engineering and Technology

detail.title: TransUNet-Based Hybrid CNN–Transformer Architecture for Precise Plant Leaf Disease Segmentation and Classification
detail.abstract: Precise and computerized detection of plant leaf diseases in precision agriculture is a serious issue that is addressed in the study because of the visual resemblance between diseases and diverse illumination levels, as well as complicated patterns of lesions, which tend to decrease the accuracy of the classification. The models that are currently available concerning CNN-based methods are mostly based on local texture extraction and often they cannot be used to extract global contextual relationships, whereas the pure transformer-based models require a great amount of computational power and large datasets. Furthermore, most past methods are found to report high training accuracy yet stability assessment, lesion quantity and validation of generalization performance is not conducted and this leaves a distinct research gap in the robust hybrid modeling frameworks. To address these shortcomings, this study presents a hybrid CNN Transformer Architecture, using a CNN encoder to extract hierarchical features, transformer to model global attention, and U-Net like decoder to refine spatial representation. The aim is to have a high multi-class classification as well as good generalization and interpretability. The balanced dataset consisting of ten plant leaf classes was trained and validated in the model, including the maize, potato, and soybean diseases. The results obtained in the experiment show excellent performance with the validation accuracy of more than 94% and the overall test accuracy of 99.33%. The majority of the classes obtained almost the same AUC values of 1.000 and precision, recall, and F1-scores of at least 0.93 across almost all categories. The confusion matrix also demonstrates that there is little misclassification and lesion area estimation also supports the fact that the model is able to work with quantitative disease severity. The results indicate a stable, non-overfitting, and highly discriminative framework that can be used in real time smart agriculture applications and automated crop health monitoring systems.

title: Immigration Enforcement Shocks and Corporate Innovation
affiliations: and Lancaster University - Department of Accounting and Finance, Lancaster University - Management School

detail.title: Immigration Enforcement Shocks and Corporate Innovation
detail.abstract: We examine the effect of immigration enforcement on corporate innovation by studying worksite Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) raids in the United States. Exploiting the timing and geographic location of worksite raids, we employ a difference-indifferences design comparing firms headquartered near a raid to those located farther away. We find that firms exposed to nearby enforcement actions experience a significant and persistent decline in innovation, measured by both patent counts and citation-weighted indicators of quality. The effects intensify over time, consistent with the cumulative nature of the innovation process. Mechanism analyses show that affected firms reduce R&D and other discretionary investment while maintaining short-term operating efficiency, suggesting a reallocation of resources away from long-horizon, high-risk projects. The negative innovation effects are concentrated in tight labor markets and in counties with high concentrations of undocumented immigrants.

title: The ORG-DeFi Model: A Structured Operational Risk Governance Framework for Decentralized Finance Platforms Interfacing with the United States Financial System

detail.title: The ORG-DeFi Model: A Structured Operational Risk Governance Framework for Decentralized Finance Platforms Interfacing with the United States Financial System

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no financial or personal relationships that could have influenced the development of this research.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was conducted independently and did not receive external funding.

detail.abstract:
Decentralized finance (DeFi) protocols increasingly interface with the United States financial ecosystem while exhibiting structural vulnerabilities related to operational resilience, governance fragmentation, and illicit finance exposure. This paper proposes a structured Operational Risk Governance Framework tailored to decentralized financial platforms, translating established financial-sector internal control and operational risk principles into functionally equivalent governance mechanisms suitable for blockchain-based environments. The framework introduces (i) an operational risk taxonomy adapted to DeFi, (ii) an internal control governance model mapped to COSO and Basel-aligned concepts, and (iii) the ORG-DeFi Model, a scoring methodology that evaluates platforms across governance integrity, technical controls, AML and illicit finance exposure, liquidity and market stability, and transparency and monitoring.

A hypothetical lending-protocol case example illustrates application for institutional due diligence, compliance assessment, and research benchmarking. By operationalizing governance indicators that align with U.S. policy priorities on financial stability, market integrity, and illicit finance mitigation, this work provides an implementation-oriented methodology to support responsible innovation and strengthen risk governance in decentralized systems.

title: Reconstructing a Century of U.S. Corporate Bonds: Credit Risk in Historical Perspective
affiliations: University of Kansas - School of Business, University of Wisconsin-Madison, University of Pennsylvania - The Wharton School and University of Wisconsin-Madison

detail.title: Reconstructing a Century of U.S. Corporate Bonds: Credit Risk in Historical Perspective
detail.abstract: Do corporate bond investors earn compensation for bearing credit risk? We construct a new historical corporate bond database spanning 128 years, from 1895 to 2022, which allows us to estimate a corporate bond counterpart to the equity risk premium. Combining hand-collected monthly corporate bond quotes from three archival print sources with modern datasets, we assemble a panel comprising over 100,000 unique bonds and more than 7 million observations. While evidence from recent samples suggests that corporate bond excess returns are driven largely by the term premium similar to that earned by U.S. Treasuries, our longer historical sample reveals a sizable and statistically significant credit risk premium. Aggregate credit spreads predict future corporate bond returns and macroeconomic aggregates, although their predictive power for business cycle fluctuations weakens when prewar data, including the Great Depression, are added.

title: Do Market Reforms Cause Growth?
affiliations: Stanford University and UCLA - Anderson School of Management

detail.title: Do Market Reforms Cause Growth?
detail.abstract: Do market-oriented economic reforms cause higher economic growth? This paper revisits the long-standing debate on the growth effects of market liberalization using crosscountry panel evidence on structural reforms. We construct a dataset combining measures of market reforms-including trade liberalization, capital account liberalization, and broader institutional reforms-with quarterly real GDP per capita growth across countries. To estimate the dynamic effects of reforms, we employ distributed-lag and autoregressive distributed-lag panel models with country and time fixed effects. The empirical framework allows us to trace the evolution of growth following reform episodes while accounting for persistence in output dynamics and global shocks. Our results indicate that market reforms are associated with positive but gradual increases in per-capita GDP growth. The effects are small in the short run but accumulate over time, suggesting that liberalization operates through slow-moving channels such as investment, productivity improvements, and institutional adjustment. These findings are broadly consistent with prior evidence that market-oriented reforms can support long-run growth, though their benefits often materialize only with substantial lags and may involve short-term adjustment costs.

detail.abstract: The explosive rise of Embodied AI and gateway-centric agents, such as OpenClaw, has evolved Large Language Models (LLMs) from mere conversational brains into operational hubs with physical execution rights and long-term memory. However, as AI extends its reach into zero-tolerance domains like smart manufacturing and low-altitude economy, the inherent absolute hallucinations of LLMs pose fatal physical threats. Our recent empirical audit reveals a severe 6.0% "Semantic Sorting Collapse" in the latest models under highly structured decision-making, demonstrating that scaling laws and RLHF cannot guarantee absolute safety in the physical world. In this position paper, we propose a pure mathematical defense architecture: the Topo-Shield. By migrating the neuro-symbolic manifold technology of HoloAuditor from the medical domain to industrial scenarios, we introduce HoloBlocker to construct a three-layer mathematical firewall comprising a Semantic Gatekeeper, a Physical Tether, and a Memory Scavenger. Combined with the Hetao XDataTrust edge-compliance framework, this architecture achieves zero-latency (0.82ms) logical auditing, providing the first mathematically provable safety foundation-a topological circuit breaker-for the large-scale deployment of Embodied AI in the real world.

detail.title: Rural America's Philanthropic Sector: Grantmaking and The Role of Philanthropy in Rural Communities
detail.abstract: Philanthropic organizations provide a key source of flexible financial investment in the form of grantmaking in the United States. As a source of capital, grants can support feasibility studies and pilot programs, serve as matching funds for other resources, and act as loss-absorbing capital to mitigate risk and entice for-profit investment. Using data from the Internal Revenue Service, we develop a novel definition for philanthropic grantmaking organizations and examine geographic differences in access to philanthropic resources between urban and rural communities. We find that, while total grantmaking averaged $116 billion per year from 2014 to 2021, just 3.5% came from rural-based organizations. We also find that a larger share of public charities is based in rural communities and those public charities issue more in grants than private foundations when compared on a per-organization basis. This has important implications for practitioners seeking out philanthropic sources of investment for their communities.

detail.abstract: The literature on urban governance and smart city enterprises underlines the growing influence of market-compelled strategies in shaping urban development. Since its commencement in 2015, India’s Smart Cities Mission has accumulated huge academic concern, principally for its prominence on entrepreneurial governance, public-private partnerships, as well as technological integration. While many analyses highlight the Mission’s potential to improve infrastructure and service delivery, scholars likewise raise concerns about spiralling socio-economic disparities, administrative inefficiencies, and the privatisation of essential urban services. This literature review critically examines the core debates encircling the Smart Cities Mission, attracting on its capacity to promote inclusivity, efficiency, and accountability in urban governance. It integrates theoretical frameworks such as smart governance, competitive and cooperative federalism, innovation-led economic growth, and modern urban planning. By situating India’s approach within broader global urbanisation trends, the review contextualises its policy ambitions and challenges. Empirical studies on infrastructure, citizen participation, and policy implementation are combined, with particular concentration on Newtown, Kolkata, as a representative case. By recognising research gaps and priority areas for future exploration, this review provided knowledge to academics concerned with smart city governance. Eventually, it upholds the need for sustainable, inclusive, and citizen-pivotal urban development strategies to guarantee enduring progress and equity in smart city enterprises.

detail.abstract: Background: Global smartphone penetration exceeds 80% in many regions, with young adults demonstrating the highest usage, frequently surpassing 4-6 hours daily. Prolonged smartphone use in flexed-head posture is associated with increased cervical and thoracic flexion, altered lumbar lordosis, and elevated neck and back pain prevalence. However, whole-spine intersegmental coordination deficits and lumbo-pelvic instability in habitual smartphone users remain underexplored[1][2][3][4][5]. Objective: To investigate the effect of an 8-week multi-segment motor control training program on spinal intersegmental coordination and lumbo-pelvic stability in young adult smartphone users with postural dysfunction. Methods: This single-center, parallel-group, assessor-blinded randomized controlled trial will recruit 80 young adults (18-35 years) using smartphones >4 hours daily and reporting neck discomfort or postural dysfunction. Participants will be randomly assigned to an experimental group receiving multi-segment motor control training (cervical, thoracic, lumbo-pelvic coordination emphasis) or a control group receiving conventional stretching, strengthening, and ergonomic education. Primary outcomes include intersegmental coordination indices derived from three-dimensional motion capture during standardized spinal movement tasks. Secondary outcomes comprise thoracic mobility, lumbo-pelvic stability (pressure biofeedback, prone instability test), neck-related disability (Neck Disability Index), pain intensity (numeric rating scale), and static spinal posture assessment. Assessments will be conducted at baseline, post-intervention (8 weeks), and 12-week follow-up. Hypotheses: The experimental group will demonstrate greater improvements in intersegmental coordination, reduced cervical segment dominance, increased thoracic mobility, and enhanced lumbo-pelvic stability compared with the control group, with moderate-to-large effect sizes (Cohen's d ≥ 0.5). Expected outcomes: If effective, multi-segment motor control training may represent a targeted rehabilitative strategy to restore whole-spine coordination and mitigate smartphone-related lumbo-pelvic instability and neck-related disability in young adults.

detail.abstract:
Background and Objectives: Parents are often the first to recognize deterioration in children, yet concern expressed under uncertainty can be interpreted in different ways. This study examined how parental concern, distress, persistence, and caregiver health knowledge were represented in New Zealand public child-health and medico-legal documents, and when those features appeared to affect parental credibility or trigger suspicion.

Methods: This qualitative document study analyzed a purposive public New Zealand corpus. Between March 10 and March 13, 2026, a single author searched the Health and Disability Commissioner decisions repository and guidance pages, Oranga Tamariki practice and research pages, and targeted Google results restricted to those domains. Seventeen records were logged; 1 live criminal matter was quarantined; 3 peripheral records were excluded; and 13 documents were retained for analysis. Detailed extraction and coding began after a 2-week washout from screening. Generative artificial intelligence tools were used for drafting support, editing, and file preparation; all source selection, analysis, verification, and final approval remained the responsibility of the author.

Results: The final corpus contained 9 Health and Disability Commissioner decisions, 1 commissioner article, 1 guidance document, and 2 Oranga Tamariki items. Four linked themes were identified. First, parental concern often became fully legible only after deterioration or diagnosis. Second, repeated presentation usually strengthened rather than weakened the case for escalation. Third, descriptors such as anxious, distressed, or exhausted were clinically ambiguous and became harmful when they slid from description into credibility judgment. Fourth, caregiver health knowledge could be read either as competence or as unusual involvement. Legitimate safeguarding concern remained real, but the documents suggested that harms arose when inferential steps from concern to suspicion were left implicit.

Conclusions: In this New Zealand document corpus, the central risk was not that parental concern was absent from the record, but that its status changed over time. Pediatric services may reduce avoidable harm by making explicit how concern is weighed, separating observed affect from motive inference, and requiring clear justification when credibility becomes part of the case.

title: EGM n: The Sequential Endogenous Grid Method

detail.title: EGM n: The Sequential Endogenous Grid Method
detail.abstract: Heterogeneous agent models with multiple decisions face a computational dilemma. Joint optimization over all choices is slow; strong separability restrictions speed computation but rule out economically interesting interactions. This paper resolves this tension through sequential decomposition. Economically simultaneous decisions need not be computationally joint. Decomposing problems into sequential stages allows each stage to exploit the Endogenous Grid Method's efficiency, chaining speed gains across decisions. The resulting non-rectilinear grids require interpolation methods that respect their structure. We develop ENGINE (ENdogenous Grid INterpolation and Extrapolation), a sequential interpolation algorithm requiring no preprocessing and no triangulation, which exploits the index structure inherited from exogenous grids. The combined method avoids optimization at stages where separable utility or invertible transitions permit EGM inversion. Benchmarks show 2-3x speedups over existing curvilinear interpolation, with simpler implementation and natural parallelization.

detail.title: Using Deep Learning and Finite-Difference Methods Together to Solve Heterogeneous Agent Models with Aggregate Shocks1
detail.abstract: This paper develops a global solution method for heterogeneous-agent macroeconomic models with aggregate shocks in environments with a large but finite number of households. The approach combines finite-difference techniques to solve the household problem with deep learning to approximate the dependence of the value function on the high-dimensional distributional state, exploiting permutation invariance across households. The algorithm is portable across model classes and readily adaptable to continuous-time models that can be solved using finite-difference methods. We illustrate the method by solving three canonical models: the Aiyagari model, the Krusell–Smith model, and a two-asset model with realistic heterogeneity in marginal propensities to consume, requiring only minimal changes to the algorithm across models. In the Krusell–Smith model, our solution closely matches the standard linear forecasting-rule approach. In contrast, in the two-asset model, aggregate dynamics differ substantially, suggesting that linear forecasting rules may not be suitable for models with realistic marginal propensities to consume and may lead to inaccurate policy and welfare conclusions.

detail.abstract: Digital health regulation has reached a critical inflection point as developments in technology outpace governance. A perceived AI-powered revolution in diagnostics, testing, and therapeutics promises transformative patient outcomes, but only if we can distinguish safe, effective applications from dangerous ones. Limitations of current regulatory guidance forces healthcare providers into an impossible choice: embrace untested innovations and shoulder unquantified risks, or reject advances that could save lives. On a national level, governments are facing a challenge to be nimble whilst safe. Digital health technology failures make headlines and when they do, providers (not suppliers or even the notified bodies that approved them) bear the legal and financial consequences. In this paper an overview is provided of the current landscape and possible future trajectories of digital health regulation. Digital health technologies are evolving quickly and their failure modes not yet sufficiently understood to align with existing regulatory definitions. For instance, whether a technology qualifies as Software as a Medical Device is the wrong question, and rigid categorisation may even cause harm. What matters is whether risks are adequately understood and mitigated. The authors propose that we can learn from other sectors facing similar challenges and adopt independent, risk-based assurance to better reflect the uncertain outcomes that they will introduce. This can help accelerate medical progress, avoiding unsafe applications and bureaucratic overreach.

detail.abstract: Colonial rule in Africa introduced health care systems in response to Africa’s disease environment. This paper analyses the spatial diffusion of colonial health care facilities in Ghana and Côte d’Ivoire through a mixed methodology. The results of the historical source analysis, based on descriptions in colonial medical reports, suggest that a range of factors influenced the locational choice of both colonizers (including European presence and economic importance), with French colonial policymakers considering a wider variety of factors than the British. The findings of the econometric analysis, using a new dataset on colonial health care facilities, support this suggested dichotomy.

detail.title: A linear-rational multi-curve term structure model with stochastic spread
detail.abstract: This study develops a linear-rational multi-curve term structure model based on the Wishart affine process. The model allows for a stochastic correlation between the curves, while the pricing of swaptions remains on par in terms of numerical complexity with caps and floors. We also show how the constant maturity swap (CMS) can be computed up to a one-dimensional integration and how the CMS option can be priced through an efficient Monte Carlo method. We provide swaption option price approximations that are fast to evaluate. These approximations heavily rely on the moments of the Wishart process, which can be computed by solving simple ordinary differential equations. This result relies on the affine property of the process. We illustrate how the model performs on real data by rolling a calibration using a 4-month long sample of at-the-money swaption data. We find that the estimated parameters are remarkably stable and the calibration procedure is robust. In particular, thanks to the specific properties of the Wishart process, the model can handle the stochastic correlation between the overnight interest swap (OIS) term structure and the Euribor-OIS spread term structure.

title: Gender, Dignity, and Equality under the ICCPR: Shadow Report to the Human Rights Committee (CCPR)

detail.title: Gender, Dignity, and Equality under the ICCPR: Shadow Report to the Human Rights Committee (CCPR)
detail.abstract: This follow-up submission evaluates India's implementation of the Human Rights Committee's Concluding Observations adopted after its fourth periodic review under the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR). It focuses on the extent to which gender equality, dignity, and substantive access to civil and political rights have been realized in law and in practice. While India maintains constitutional guarantees of equality and non-discrimination, significant gaps persist between formal commitments and lived realities for women and girls. The report identifies four interrelated areas of concern. First, indirect discrimination and fragmented enforcement mechanisms continue to undermine substantive equality under Articles 2, 3, and 26 of the Covenant. Gender-neutral legal frameworks often fail to account for structural disadvantage, and the absence of consistent sex-disaggregated data limits oversight and accountability. Second, the State's response to gender-based violence reflects persistent failures in prevention, investigation, and access to remedies, engaging India's positive obligations under Articles 2, 6, and 7. Impunity, underreporting, and uneven availability of survivor support services remain systemic challenges. Third, policies and institutional practices affecting bodily autonomy and privacy disproportionately impact women, raising concerns under Articles 7 and 17. Safeguards related to informed consent and confidentiality are inconsistently applied, particularly for marginalized populations. Fourth, gendered barriers to civic participation, including harassment, restrictions on assembly, and underrepresentation in decision-making, continue to limit the effective exercise of rights protected under Articles 19, 21, and 25. The submission proposes targeted, measurable recommendations aligned with the Committee's follow-up procedures, aimed at strengthening implementation and improving institutional coordination, to ensure meaningful accountability for gender-related ICCPR obligations.

detail.title: The Role of Country-by-Country Reporting (CbCR) in Curbing Tax Avoidance
detail.abstract: This research investigates the role of Country-by-Country Reporting (CbCR) in curbing tax avoidance, focusing on the effectiveness of its implementation in multinational corporations. The study analyzes the impact of CbCR on tax transparency and corporate tax compliance, with a specific focus on developing economies. The findings suggest that while CbCR increases transparency, its effect on reducing tax avoidance is limited by gaps in enforcement and international cooperation. The study concludes that CbCR has the potential to reduce tax avoidance but requires stronger regulatory frameworks and enforcement mechanisms to be more effective.

detail.abstract: Contemporary antitrust debates are increasingly characterized by per-sistent disagreement over empirical evidence, methodological standards, and en-forcement priorities. In this Article I argue that these conflicts cannot be fully explained as ordinary methodological disputes. They can be explained by differing ideological viewpoints either. Building on earlier work on the so-called “crisis” of antitrust economics and the psychology of antitrust agencies, I show how insights from the literatures on moralized judgment, motivated reasoning, and fact polari-zation can help explain why antitrust disagreement has become intractable and re-sistant to evidence; why methodological debates are merely instrumental; and ideological differences cannot be bridged. When antitrust reasoning shifts from consequentialist analysis toward moral condemnation of market power and firm’s size, traditional legal constraints lose their disciplining function. The result is greater enforcement discretion, doctrinal instability, and declining institutional le-gitimacy. Rather than advocating particular enforcement outcomes, I offer an insti-tutional diagnosis and identify legal design principles—epistemic restraint, procedural discipline, and structured judicial review—that could allow antitrust law to function effectively in a polarized environment.

title: Lighting up the Future: Electricity Shortage Alleviation and Intergenerational Educational Mobility in Rural China

detail.title: Lighting up the Future: Electricity Shortage Alleviation and Intergenerational Educational Mobility in Rural China
detail.abstract: Promoting intergenerational educational mobility is widely considered to be a crucial foundation for achieving long-term social equity and inclusive growth. Although electricity supply is a vital driver of social development, rigorous causal evidence remains scarce regarding its actual impact on improving long-term educational opportunities for disadvantaged groups’ descendants. Using county-level cohort data from over 200,000 parent–offspring pairs and leveraging China’s phased rural electrification reforms during the 1980s and 1990s as a quasi-natural experiment, we employ a cohort difference-in-differences model to identify the causal effects of electricity shortage alleviation on rural intergenerational educational mobility. Our findings reveal that electricity shortage alleviation from electrification policies significantly reduced the next generation’s survival and developmental constraints, resulting in a 23.1% decrease in the correlation between parental and offspring educational attainment. This effect was more pronounced in regions and groups facing stronger socioeconomic constraints, natural endowment and geographic limitations, and intrahousehold resource allocation constraints, highlighting the influence of electricity as a public good on addressing market failures. Furthermore, an expanded analysis beyond the individual level indicates that rural electrification significantly improves the regional structure of educational opportunities, mitigates the relationship between intergenerational educational mobility and inequality, and demonstrates a high cost–benefit ratio. Our research confirms that alleviating electricity shortages can reshape the structure of educational opportunities, with profound long-term impacts on social mobility and inequality patterns.

title: Arunachala Gounder (Dead) v. Ponnuswamy: Redefining Succession and Coparcenary Rights of Hindu Daughters

detail.title: Arunachala Gounder (Dead) v. Ponnuswamy: Redefining Succession and Coparcenary Rights of Hindu Daughters
detail.abstract: This paper delves into the complex and evolving landscape of succession and coparcenary rights for Hindu daughters in India, with a particular focus on the significant judgment in Arunachala Gounder (dead) v Ponnuswamy in January 2022. The paper aims to shed light on the prevailing legal provisions governing the inheritance and management rights of Hindu women, including daughters, and scrutinizes recent judicial trends that have sought to enhance these rights. The paper also seeks to elucidate the jurisprudential significance of the Arunachala Gounder case within the broader context of succession and coparcenary rights for Hindu daughters. In a country where gender equality and women's rights have garnered increasing attention, understanding and safeguarding the rights of Hindu daughters in matters of property and inheritance is of paramount importance. The paper navigates through the intricacies of succession and coparcenary rights and the transformative impact of legislative changes, particularly the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act of 2005. Through a comprehensive examination of these legal provisions and their practical implications, this paper provides a guide to navigate the rights of Hindu daughters, emphasizing their entitlement to both inherit and manage joint family property. It underscores the importance of recognizing the evolving legal framework and dispelling misconceptions that may hinder the exercise of these rights.

title: Diagnosing Adoption Dynamics: A Structural Approach to Diffusion Modeling

detail.title: Diagnosing Adoption Dynamics: A Structural Approach to Diffusion Modeling
detail.abstract: Why do identical product launches succeed rapidly in some markets while languishing in others? Managers facing sluggish adoption confront a diagnostic challenge: does the problem reect population composition (too few early adopters to spark momentum) or weak signaling (insucient visibility of early adoption)? Standard diusion models cannot answer this question because they lack micro-foundations connecting who adopts to how adoption unfolds. We develop a coordination game framework where heterogeneous consumers balance social proof (conforming to observable adoption) against aspirational imitation (following early adopters). The equilibrium yields a reduced-form specication with structurally interpretable coecients: persistence reects mass-market conformity pressure; second-order dynamics capture delayed follower response to innovator behavior; shock responsiveness depends on early adopter share and behavioral heterogeneity. This structural mapping enables root-cause diagnosis from adoption data alonedecomposing observed dynamics into composition versus signaling components and maps these diagnostics to actionable levers: whether to invest in early-adopter targeting and inuencer partnerships (composition interventions) or improve visibility and social proof (signaling interventions). We validate parameter recovery through Monte Carlo simulation and demonstrate applications spanning linguistic innovation (Google Books, 1900-2019) to online discourse (Reddit, 2024), contexts diering by ve orders of magnitude in timescale yet conforming to the same specication. The framework equips practitioners to diagnose diusion problems and design appropriately targeted interventions.

detail.abstract: This paper introduces Reserve Capacity Theory (RCT), a formal analytical framework for evaluating economic stability that departs from conventional equilibrium-based models. Rather than focusing on static performance metrics or growth trajectories, RCT examines the dynamic margin between normal operating conditions and systemic failure across multiple interdependent domains. We formalize the concept of economic reserve-the latent capacity to absorb shocks, adapt to changing conditions, and maintain function under stress-and demonstrate how its depletion creates nonlinear vulnerability that remains invisible to traditional macroeconomic indicators. The framework contributes three principal innovations: (1) a multidimensional reserve capacity function with formally specified cross-domain coupling dynamics and endogenous threshold evolution; (2) a rigorous treatment of the observational divergence between headline economic performance and latent systemic fragility; and (3) a political economy model explaining systematic reserve under-provision in democratic systems. Applying this framework to the contemporary U.S. economy, and validating it through a detailed case study of global repo market vulnerabilities identified by the Financial Stability Board, reveals structural fragilities masked by strong headline performance. We demonstrate that RCT nests several prominent results in the systemic risk literature-including the phase-transition results of Acemoglu, Ozdaglar, and Tahbaz-Salehi (2015) and the antifragility framework of Taleb (2012)-within a unified analytical structure, while extending them to multi-domain economic analysis with endogenous institutional dynamics.

title: The Paradox of Control How US Semiconductor Export Restrictions Are Reshaping China's Technological Sovereignty
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: The Paradox of Control How US Semiconductor Export Restrictions Are Reshaping China's Technological Sovereignty
detail.abstract: US export controls on advanced semiconductors, implemented in October 2022 to constrain China's technological development, have produced paradoxical outcomes that complicate strategic assessments of their effectiveness. This paper studies how these restrictions are altering China's semiconductor industry and their consequences on technical sovereignty through 2033. Employing a combined methodology integrating production capacity, trade flows, and innovation metrics, the study shows that although export controls have successfully constrained access to state-of-the-art fabrication capabilities, they have simultaneously catalyzed reorientation toward mature-node production and intensified domestic innovation. Main findings consist of SMIC's 84.6 percent revenue spike and 7nm production achievement, Huawei's 90 percent domestic component localization, and China's projected majority self-sufficiency in mature nodes by 2030. The analysis validates the "creative insecurity" framework: external pressure has stimulated rather than suppressed Chinese semiconductor development by redirecting industrial policy and creating imperatives for technology substitution. However, dependence on foreign equipment for advanced nodes constrains frontier capabilities through 2030. The emerging two-tiered ecosystem-Chinese dominance in mature nodes, US advantage at the frontier-represents partial success and partial failure, with unintended consequences including supply chain bifurcation and erosion of US leverage. The evidence indicates that in sectors with rapid innovation, substantial state capacity, and large domestic markets, technology denial strategies face intrinsic limitations and may inadvertently accelerate rival autonomy while achieving intended constraints.

title: The Limits of Rational Inattention: Large Shocks and State-Dependent Pricing in Emerging Markets
affiliations: Istanbul Bilgi University and Florida International University (FIU) - Department of Economics

detail.title: The Limits of Rational Inattention: Large Shocks and State-Dependent Pricing in Emerging Markets
detail.abstract: Standard New Keynesian models often treat information frictions as structural primitives that generate a stable zone of inaction. This paper challenges that universality by documenting the endogenous collapse of the inattention shield during a transition from price stability to high inflation. Using a high-frequency panel of weekly retail prices from Istanbul, Türkiye between 2005 and 2026, we identify a regime shift governed by an endogenously estimated inflation threshold. In the low-inflation regime, price adjustments are time-dependent with flat hazard functions, consistent with rational inattention. However, once the inflation drift breaches the critical threshold, the pricing technology switches fundamentally. We uncover the emergence of sharp V-shaped hazard functions, confirming that large shocks compel firms to switch to state-dependent rules driven by physical menu costs. This transition generates a nonlinear hockey stick Phillips curve, where the aggregate frequency of adjustment becomes highly sensitive to inflation drift. Notably, we find this regime switch is most dramatic in modern supermarkets, debunking the view that organizational rigidity is invariant to the aggregate environment. Our findings empirically validate the dual-friction framework and demonstrate that the zone of inaction is a fragile equilibrium outcome that vanishes in volatile environments.

title: Do Environmental Payments Retire Productive Cropland? Evidence from England’s Countryside Stewardship Scheme
affiliations: University of Cambridge

detail.title: Do Environmental Payments Retire Productive Cropland? Evidence from England’s Countryside Stewardship Scheme
detail.abstract: The United Kingdom’s shift from area-based farm subsidies to outcome-contingent environmental contracting represents a major change in agricultural policy. While these schemes aim to improve environmental outcomes, their effects on land allocation within the agricultural production frontier remain poorly understood. Using high-resolution land-cover data and the staggered rollout of England’s Countryside Stewardship Scheme, this paper estimates dynamic treatment effects on holding-level land-use shares. Participation significantly reduces arable cereal area, including on highly productive soils, with persistent conversion into grassland and other non-arable uses. These results indicate that agri-environmental payments induce land reallocation rather than simply altering management practices. Linking these land-use responses to a carbon-accounting framework, we show that displaced domestic cereal production can generate economically meaningful carbon-leakage risks under plausible assumptions about trade and livestock adjustment.

title: Dynamic Sorting in the Coastal Housing Market - Who Surfs the Tide, Who Bears the Brunt?
affiliations: Virginia Tech, University of Connecticut - Department of Agricultural and Resource Economics and the National Center for Smart Growth and North Carolina State University - Department of Agricultural and Resource Economics

detail.title: Dynamic Sorting in the Coastal Housing Market - Who Surfs the Tide, Who Bears the Brunt?
detail.abstract: Flood risk and housing price volatility coexist in coastal communities, yet their interaction remains understudied, limiting understanding of household locational choices. This paper develops a dynamic sorting model to capture heterogeneous household preferences for coastal amenities and risks, enabling simulations of residential mobility under alternative coastal policies. Estimates of marginal willingness to pay reveal systematic variation in preference and behavioral patterns across ethnicity, economic conditions, and housing market cycles. During the pre-recession housing bubble, households substantially underestimated flood risk. After the recession, the value placed on avoiding flood risk increased and became statistically significant for certain groups. In contrast, ocean views were consistently highly valued, and racial clustering persisted. Policy simulations indicate that the effectiveness and welfare implications of flood insurance reforms depend critically on the availability of low-risk housing. When such housing is sufficient, higher flood insurance rates increase wealth levels while reducing both overall housing demand and minority shares in flood zones, with residential sorting mitigating welfare losses. Under constrained low-risk housing supply, however, sorting mechanisms become ineffective, and rising insurance premiums impose substantial welfare losses.

title: One Hundred Years in the U.S. Stock Markets
affiliations: W.P. Carey School of Business

detail.title: One Hundred Years in the U.S. Stock Markets
