detail.abstract: This study summarizes investment outcomes for 29,754 common stocks listed in the public U.S. stock markets over the 100-year period from 1926 to 2025, reporting on both compound (buyand-hold) percentage returns and shareholder wealth enhancement measured in dollars. While the cross-stock mean buy-and-hold return is over 30,000%, the median is-6.9%. Shareholders' wealth was enhanced by $91 trillion over the century, but long-term investors in nearly 60% of stocks incurred wealth reductions. The degree to which wealth creation is concentrated in a few firms has increased sharply in recent years. Over the 1926 to 2016 period studied in Bessembinder (2018), 89 firms accounted for half of the $43 trillion in net wealth creation. After including outcomes for the most recent nine years, just 46 firms account for half of the $91 trillion in net wealth creation over the full century.

title: Concave Loss Aversion? Evidence From Real Goods
affiliations: University of Austin

detail.title: Concave Loss Aversion? Evidence From Real Goods
detail.abstract: Prospect Theory challenged Expected Utility Theory by introducing three central features: (1) reference dependence, (2) loss aversion, and (3) diminishing sensitivity in both gain and loss domains. While the first two features have been widely supported in experimental settings, this paper presents evidence that diminishing sensitivity in the loss domain may not generalize to behavior involving real consumable goods. In a novel auction experiment, hungry participants endowed with pizza slices submitted willingness-to-accept (WTA) and willingness-to-pay (WTP) bids around a reference allocation. The results confirm strong loss aversion and diminishing marginal utility in gains. However, contrary to Prospect Theory's prediction of convexity in losses (i.e., diminishing marginal sensitivity), the data exhibit increasing marginal disutility as inventory shrinks. A single smooth concave utility function fits the observed behavior across both domains, as does a Prospect Theory specification when concavity in the negative domain is allowed. These findings suggest that loss aversion does not require decreasing sensitivity to losses.

title: Rational Stein-GARCH Model: Endogenous Power-Law Tails, Bounded GMM Estimation and Risk Measures for Infinite-Kurtosis Assets

detail.title: Rational Stein-GARCH Model: Endogenous Power-Law Tails, Bounded GMM Estimation and Risk Measures for Infinite-Kurtosis Assets
detail.abstract:
Aiming at the "fourth-moment theoretical divergence" and "time-varying power-law characteristics" exhibited by extremely heavy-tailed assets such as Bitcoin, traditional financial econometric models based on Gaussian kernel modifications or relying on the existence of higher-order moments (e.g., GARCH-t) are facing the dual dilemmas of theoretical failure and risk underestimation. This study breaks through the limitations of the traditional "polynomial operator" and proposes for the first time the framework of the Rational Stein Operator. By introducing a quadratic term in the denominator, it realizes a paradigm shift of the underlying distribution generation mechanism from "superexponential decay" to "power-law decay". Theoretical proofs show that the operator can not only endogenously generate a strict power-law tail with α=1/ν, but also achieve complete decoupling of skewness and heavy-tailed parameters through the "choking mechanism". In terms of estimation strategy, this study designs the Bounded Stein-GMM method, which constructs moment conditions using bounded test functions, achieving a double breakthrough that neither requires calculating the normalization constant K nor relies on the existence of higher-order moments, ensuring the consistency and asymptotic normality of the estimator in scenarios with divergent variance.
Empirical studies based on Bitcoin, crude oil and the S&P 500 index from 2018 to 2025 show that:
1.Goodness of fit: The Rational Stein Model perfectly fits the power-law characteristics in the log-log space, with AIC/BIC significantly superior to traditional models;
2.Risk measurement: The dynamic Stein-GARCH model performs excellently in the 99.9% VaR stress test, successfully intercepting the black swan shocks on "March 12" 2020 and early 2026, with zero actual failure times;
3.Pricing logic: The dynamic tail parameter νt contributes approximately 44% of the heavy-tailed premium for deep out-of-the-money put options, effectively correcting the hedging cost bias.
This study not only provides a robust risk monitoring radar for extremely heavy-tailed assets, but also offers a new theoretical benchmark for the expansion of the Stein method in non-Gaussian fields.

title: Beyond Access: Exploring Threshold Effects of Financial Inclusion on Food Security in Africa
affiliations: University of Pretoria and University of Pretoria

detail.title: Beyond Access: Exploring Threshold Effects of Financial Inclusion on Food Security in Africa
detail.abstract: This study examines the trends and nonlinear threshold effects of financial inclusion on food security and dietary outcomes in Ethiopia, Ghana, Kenya, and South Africa, using data from the Global Findex and FAOSTAT (2014, 2017, and 2021). A multidimensional Financial Inclusion Index is constructed via Principal Component Analysis (PCA), capturing access and usage of formal financial services (account ownership, savings, credit, digital payments).,Descriptive trends reveal divergent patterns: inclusion rises with age (peaking at 30–50 years) but lags among youth due to income and exposure constraints. South Africa leads with mature infrastructure; Kenya shows strong gains via mobile money (e.g., M-Pesa); Ghana advances moderately; Ethiopia stagnates amid limited liberalization. Education exhibits counterintuitive declines in the Financial Inclusive Index, reflecting measurement bias toward basic services that underrepresent sophisticated engagement among educated groups. Income trends invert post-2016, favoring lower quintiles via pro-poor digital tools, while gender gaps narrow but persist due to literacy and employment barriers. Overall decline signals macroeconomic challenges, underscoring digital innovation's uneven impact.,Dynamic panel threshold models identify critical regimes. For food insecurity, thresholds at ~0.31 (composite index) and 0.27 (usage index) reveal steep reductions in low-inclusion regimes, –31.55 to –38.85 percentage points per unit increase, versus moderated effects in high regimes, –13.48 to –19.14 points, highlighting early-adoption gains (e.g., rural Ethiopia) and diminishing returns due to saturation (e.g., urban Kenya/South Africa). Tertiary education amplifies impacts in both regimes, likely via remittances/investments. For average dietary energy supply adequacy, a threshold at 0.3117 yields stronger early gains (+5.92 points) than later moderation (+3.77 points), with education enhancing benefits in high regimes.,Specific dynamics show declining inclusion and rising insecurity in Ethiopia, Ghana, and Kenya amid crises, contrasting South Africa's resilience. These findings emphasize financial inclusion's nonlinear, regime-dependent role in nutritional outcomes, calling for targeted digital expansion, literacy, and usage-deepening policies to maximize early gains in low-penetration contexts while addressing saturation in advanced settings.

title: The Environmental Effects of Ambient Charges in a Partially Cooperating Duopoly
affiliations: Institute for Economic Sciences

detail.title: The Environmental Effects of Ambient Charges in a Partially Cooperating Duopoly
detail.abstract: This paper explores a Cournot duopoly model involving two firms that engage in partial cooperation. The paper reevaluates the effectiveness of using ambient charges as a policy tool to control industrial nonpoint-source pollution. The findings suggest that when the level of cooperation between the firms is relatively low, increasing ambient charges can serve as an effective means to reduce pollution. By analyzing the strategic interactions between the firms, the paper highlights how limited cooperation influences the success of environmental policies. These insights contribute to a better understanding of regulatory approaches in industries where firms have interdependent pollution outcomes.

title: Interplay of Risks in Variable Annuity
affiliations: Hunan University and Nankai University

detail.title: Interplay of Risks in Variable Annuity
detail.abstract: A guaranteed variable annuity provides a guaranteed benefit to the investor, no matter what the performance of the investment account is. Although the pricing formula and hedging strategy of the guaranteed variable annuity are well-studied in the literature, the intrinsic risk transfer and diversification mechanisms between policyholder and insurer had not yet been fully recognized. In this paper, we propose a rigorous mathematical model based on classic geometric Brownian motion to describe the financial position of the policyholder and insurer in different types of guaranteed variable annuities. Both mechanisms are examined by analyzing the interplay of equity risk and mortality risk, and numerical results of the proposed model present the well-known fact that the investor gives up potential upside gain in exchange for protection from the downside loss. Moreover, the model offers some insights into practical operations. Besides, the comparison between the Black-Scholes model and the stochastic volatility jump model tells us that an unexpected jump in volatility affects the profitability of the guaranteed variable annuity.

title: Urban Expansion and LULC Change in the Addis Ababa City Periphery: Implications for Farmland Sustainability in Present-Day Sheger City
affiliations: Addis Ababa Science and Technology University, Addis Ababa University and Addis Ababa University

detail.title: Urban Expansion and LULC Change in the Addis Ababa City Periphery: Implications for Farmland Sustainability in Present-Day Sheger City
detail.abstract: Unregulated urban expansion in Ethiopia is driving significant land use/land cover (LULC) changes with critical implications for agriculture and food security. This study analyzes LULC dynamics in the Addis Ababa periphery—Sheger City—from 2003 to 2023 using multi-temporal Landsat imagery and socio-economic data. Geospatial findings were triangulated with household surveys (n = 393), FGDs, and KIIs to capture community perceptions. Results reveal sharp declines in crop land and grassland alongside rapid built-up growth: crop land fell from 74,689 ha in 2015 to 64,689 ha in 2023, while built-up expanded from 887 ha in 2003 to 36,309 ha in 2023, gaining primarily at the expense of crop land and grassland (74,303 ha → 26,380 ha). Participants linked these changes to informal/formal settlement expansion and weak land governance. Shrinking agricultural and grazing land reduced crop output, threatened livestock keeping, and increased food insecurity risks. Political-administrative dynamics also aggravated LULC changes. Findings highlight the urgent need for participatory land-use planning and policies that balance urban growth with agricultural sustainability.

title: Fast Core Identification
affiliations: Cornell University

detail.title: Fast Core Identification
detail.abstract: Digital markets are becoming increasingly diverse. Instead of bilateral trading denominated in USD, one may choose to swap digital assets for one or more sets of digital assets, real-world assets, and more, all in the same transaction. This paper proposes a fast eigenvector-based methodology to find the core of a multi-dimensional allocation. The methodology identifies the stable allocation that is incentive-compatible and strategy-proof in linear time (O(n)). In addition to digital asset swaps, the proposed technique can be well suited for complex large-dimensional problems like housing choice and school choice, among others. The process retains all the properties of Top Trading Cycles (TTC), namely Pareto efficiency, individual rationality, and strategy-proofness. * irenealdridge.com; I am grateful to Laura Doval and participants of Economics and Computation 2024 (EC2024) for valuable suggestions and advice.

detail.abstract: The net zero shift of the world has been a key goal of climate governance whereby governments strive to lower the emission of greenhouse gases without compromising the progress of the economy and stability in international trade. Nevertheless, the proliferation of climate mitigation policies has instituted escalating legal conflicts between environmental regulation and the international trade law. This paper discusses the legality of the Net Zero Strategy of the United Kingdom on the trade laws of the World Trade Organization (WTO) and more specifically on the regulation of the subsidies and the non-discriminatory laws. The study addresses the question whether green subsidies and regulatory incentives implemented in the decarbonisation strategy by the UK may potentially be incompatible with WTO requirements in the Agreement on Subsidies and Countervailing Measures and the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade. The research has a doctrinal legal research approach, alongside comparative review of the law and policy assessment. The legal framework of the trade subsidies and environmental exceptions under the WTO law is interpreted in the doctrinal analysis. Comparative analysis will be conducted to analyse the differences in the UK Net Zero Strategy and the European Union Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism because of the effort to understand how the various policy tools apply to climate targets yet remain in trade compliance. Policy analysis also looks at the economics and regulation of green industrial policies concerning the global climate governance. The results show that even though the climate mitigation policies can be of concern due to their potential to cause distortion in trade they can be compatible with the international trade law whenever they do not seek other motives other than environmental protection and are applied in a non-discriminatory and reasonable way. The environmental exceptions of WTO especially the ones concerning environmental protection and conservation of resources give significant legal assistance that enables governments to implement climate policies without necessarily breaking trade. The paper finds that ambitious policies aimed at combating climate change should be cautiously developed with international regulatory alignment, in order to keep track of global trade regulations.

title: Journal WEB Supplement for "Systems Analysis of Decision-Making under Ambiguity with Comparative Out-of-Sample Experimental Study of Geometric Dispersion Theory & Cumulative Prospect Theory"
affiliations: Case Western Reserve University - School of Engineering and Case Western Reserve University - Case Western Reserve University, Computer Science

detail.title: Journal WEB Supplement for "Systems Analysis of Decision-Making under Ambiguity with Comparative Out-of-Sample Experimental Study of Geometric Dispersion Theory & Cumulative Prospect Theory"
detail.abstract: In this paper, we develop a new descriptive model for ambiguity decision-making called Ambiguity Geometric Dispersion Theory (A-GDT). In out-of-sample predictions, we find that A-GDT is experimentally superior to all models which it generalizes; specifically, cumulative prospect theory (CPT), subjective expected utility (SEU), alpha-maxmin expected utility (α-MEU), vector expected utility (VEU), and expected utility theory (EUT). We ran an experimental study of 150 decisions under ambiguity by 310 subjects by operationalizing payoffs, probability, and ambiguity. We show that subjects exhibit behavior that contradicts many decision models, such as CPT, SEU, α-MEU, and EUT; but not A-GDT. In out-of-sample studies with the same number of parameters, the A-GDT model predicts both representative (aggregate) agent and individual preferences substantially better than other well-known ambiguity models. Specifically, a three-parameter A-GDT is substantially superior to CPT and all other important models. Furthermore, significance testing in a paired comparison of models shows that subjects' behavior matches the A-GDT model markedly better than other models. A new rate-of-degradation analysis demonstrates that A-GDT's predictions are far more stable than other models as the insample size is decreased. In addition, the A-GDT model not only can resolve typical Ellsberg-like behavior, but it can also resolve hypothetical and real-life ambiguity problems with multiple sources of ambiguity including the paradoxes by Machina.

title: Nature's Pharmacy in Peril: Redirecting Biomedicine Revenues for Biodiversity Conservation
affiliations: Phenikaa University, Widya Mandala Surabaya Catholic University and Phenikaa University

detail.title: Nature's Pharmacy in Peril: Redirecting Biomedicine Revenues for Biodiversity Conservation
detail.abstract: Biomedicine increasingly powers global health and economies, yet its innovation pipeline remains fundamentally dependent on biodiversity which supplies natural products and inspiration for modern drugs. Meanwhile, the extinction rates accelerate and conservation finance lags. Based on the semiconducting principle of environmental and monetary value, this perspective proposes an actionable mechanism to redirect a fraction of biomedicine’s revenues toward conservation. Embedding these tools can foster an eco-surplus culture in which every life-saving therapy contributes to safeguarding species and habitats, securing innovation and planetary health.

title: Unveiling Risk on Bank Balance Sheets: From Risk Disclosure to Credit Reallocation
affiliations: Bocconi University - Department of Finance and

detail.title: Unveiling Risk on Bank Balance Sheets: From Risk Disclosure to Credit Reallocation

publicationDetails.journalName: BAFFI Centre on Economics, Finance & Regulation Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: We examine how banks adjust credit allocation when hidden credit risk is revealed. Using supervisory risk disclosure data from the European Central Bank's 2014 Asset Quality Review, we find that banks experiencing larger increases in non-performing loans and provisions significantly reduce riskweighted exposures while keeping total credit volumes largely unchanged. This suggests that derisking primarily occurs through portfolio reallocation-particularly within portfolios-rather than through credit contraction. We document heterogeneous responses depending on the rating approach used to measure credit risk and we show that capital constraints amplify, but are not the sole drivers of, de-risking. Finally, we provide evidence that supervisory risk disclosure plays a key role in shaping banks' risk-taking behavior, even in the absence of observable adjustments in their financial statements.

detail.abstract: This research paper analyzes how several macroeconomic indicators, representing major segments of the economy, affect the stock performance of three largecap technology firms: Microsoft, Apple, and Amazon. These companies, purposefully chosen for this study, are highly liquid yet have some of the largest market caps because their monthly earnings correlate with prominent indicators of GDP, inflation, employment, housing, and trade balances. Using publicly available data sources from government departments and international institutions is what makes this study's claims, real-time economic fluctuations, and facts verifiable and credible. This study uses a quantitative framework to analyze, in depth, the correlation between macroeconomic indicators and stock performance during the 2022-2023 post-pandemic time period. Key findings in this study demonstrate trends and patterns in GDP growth, inflation, and employment. Since measurements such as the CPI and PPI fluctuate, macroeconomic indicators are closely associated with stock movements. It is extremely important to all traders and investors around the world, from small family households to the largest firms, to place a high emphasis on analyzing macroeconomic dynamics and evaluating equity performance. The analysis of these essential indicators is very insightful and decisive for investors and traders who use a framework to interpret what economic indicators mean and which strategies can be used to price action on those indicators in tech-driven markets.

detail.title: A Health-Economic Assessment of the impact of different RSVpreF maternal vaccine strategies to prevent RSV infections among young infants, in France: EPIPACT
detail.abstract: ObjectivesMost of pediatric Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) burden involves infants aged <1 year. Since 2024, RSVpreF vaccine is available in France for the vaccination of pregnant women, from September to January. This study aimed to model the impact of alternative RSVpreF national vaccination strategies on RSV hospital burden.MethodsA three-state Markov model – Susceptible, RSV-related hospitalization, Death – was developed. The 627,499 annual births modeled were split in two cohorts of infants born to vaccinated and unvaccinated women. Four strategies were modeled: no vaccination, vaccination between September and January (recommended), between May and January (extended), and year-round. Results were presented at a population level using a healthcare perspective, as cost per hospitalization avoided, and number needed to vaccinate (NNV).ResultsWithout vaccination, 38,625 RSV-related hospitalizations among infants <1 year were estimated annually, costing €120.0 million (M). Recommended strategy prevented 7,620 (-19.7%) hospitalizations, 90.4% of them involved infants aged <3 months (99.5% aged <6 months). The related total cost was €126.4M, corresponding to €844 per hospitalization avoided, and an NNV of 21 vaccinations to avoid one hospitalization. Compared to the recommended strategy, the extended strategy avoided an additional 4,111 (-13.3%) hospitalizations, 42.0% in infants aged <3 months (95.0% aged <6 months). The total cost of this strategy was €134.4M (+6.3%), corresponding to €1,929 per additional hospitalization avoided. Total cost of the year-round strategy was €156.2M, for 1,306 additional hospitalizations avoided.ConclusionsThis is the first cost-effectiveness model to describe the impact of alternative vaccination strategies for RSV prevention in France. Between 7,600 (recommended) and >13,000 (year-round) hospitalizations were avoided with vaccination, corresponding to hospital savings between €24.7M and €41.5M. Alternative scenarii tended to extend prevention to older age groups. Broader vaccination strategies, notably extended strategy, had a positive impact on RSV hospital burden, with a limited impact on costs.

title: Nature as Mentor: Biomimicry Education and Communication for Nature Quotient Cultivation and Eco-surplus Development
affiliations: Phenikaa University, Vietnam Academy of Social Sciences - Institute of Philosophy and Phenikaa University

detail.title: Nature as Mentor: Biomimicry Education and Communication for Nature Quotient Cultivation and Eco-surplus Development
detail.abstract: Humanity’s survival depends on the health of natural systems, yet prevailing measures of intelligence fail to guide truly sustainable behavior. Nature Quotient (NQ)—the capacity to perceive and act upon the interdependence of humans and nature—offers a pathway to cultivate an eco-surplus culture in which societies generate net positive ecological impacts. This paper argues that biomimicry is both a tangible expression of humanity’s reliance on biodiversity and a powerful tool for fostering NQ. Drawing on Granular Interaction Thinking Theory (GITT), we conceptualize how communicating nature-inspired innovations can reconfigure individuals’ information–value nexuses, embedding ecological awareness into decision-making. We review biomimicry’s expanding influence across education, design, engineering, and policy, and outline multi-level strategies—integrating biomimicry into formal curricula, citizen science, communication, and innovation networks—to elevate NQ across society. By systematically embedding “nature as mentor” in learning and public discourse, these strategies can drive a cultural shift from eco-deficit to eco-surplus, enhancing collective capacity for nature-based innovation, serendipity, and regenerative development.

title: From Nature-Inspired Innovation to Nature Conservation and Restoration Financing
affiliations: Phenikaa University, Phenikaa University and Phenikaa University

detail.title: From Nature-Inspired Innovation to Nature Conservation and Restoration Financing
detail.abstract: Biomimicry—the practice of emulating nature’s time-tested patterns and strategies—has yielded transformative innovations across sectors, from energy-efficient transport to advanced materials and medical devices. Yet this rapid growth in nature-inspired innovation unfolds against the backdrop of an accelerating biodiversity crisis. This paradox highlights an “innovation debt” to nature: humanity benefits from ecosystems’ intellectual capital while their degradation undermines the very knowledge base upon which future solutions depend. This perspective advances a profit-sharing mechanism to reinvest a portion of biomimicry-derived revenues into biodiversity conservation and restoration. Grounded in the semiconducting principle—which permits conversion of environmental value into monetary gain but prohibits monetary gain from offsetting environmental loss—the model operationalizes benefit-sharing through a five-step process: identification, contribution calculation, payment and pooling, allocation, and accountability. Contributions, proportionate to commercial success, would be directed to priority projects, with allocations reflecting both the origin of inspiration and conservation urgency. The proposed framework can help address the biodiversity finance gap, embed nature as a stakeholder in enterprise, and foster an eco-surplus culture in which business success and ecological regeneration advance together. In doing so, it creates a feedback loop where the more we innovate like nature, the more we invest in sustaining it.

title: The Phantom of "Q-Variance": A Measurement Artefact of the Daily Reporting Grid
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The Phantom of "Q-Variance": A Measurement Artefact of the Daily Reporting Grid
detail.abstract: It is well known that, in quantum mechanics, the act of measurement can affect the outcome. This study argues that the empirical regularity termed "q-variance"-a fixed-horizon relation between normalized realized log-returns and realized variance in which the slope coefficient is constrained exactly to 1/2-is a sampling-induced artefact of the close-to-close observation scheme rather than a fundamental market property. While standard continuous-time, diffusion-based pricing and hedging models typically abstract from calendar-and session-induced sampling effects, the analysis shows that these models can be extended transparently by introducing a class of processes, termed gated càdlàg semimartingales, to incorporate such market microstructure frictions without resorting to a "quantum-theoretic narrative".

detail.abstract: Power generation from renewable energy has been increasing in recent years, although its inherent uncertainty potentially undermines supply stability. Therefore, power generation from non-renewable energy is expected to remain necessary, albeit at a reduced level. From this perspective, we examine a fuel procurement problem for a non-renewable power generator that maximizes the expected total discounted profit over an infinite horizon. Our problem is formulated as a continuous-time stochastic linear quadratic (LQ) control problem. In our model, renewable generation is described by an inhomogeneous geometric Brownian motion to ensure non-negativity and bounded expectation. By examining the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) equation, our theoretical results show that the optimal fuel procurement strategy for the nonrenewable power generator becomes an affine function of renewable generation, electricity price volatility, and the fuel inventory level. We also provide a sufficient condition under which the verification theorem holds for our stochastic LQ problem. Furthermore, our numerical experiments illustrate several important points. In particular, non-renewable power generators decrease their fuel procurement speed, particularly when both renewable policy targets and technological progress in renewable generation are high. Moreover, in the long run, price volatility has a stronger impact on the fuel procurement strategy than uncertainty in renewable generation.

detail.abstract: Macroprudential policies (MaPs) have become the centrepiece of the post-GFC regulatory financial stability architecture, yet evidence on their firm-level consequences remains fragmented across banking, macroeconomics and corporate finance. This paper provides an integrative review of micro evidence on the transmission of MaPs to corporate financing and firms' economic decisions, organised around a stylised three-period theoretical framework with collateral constraints and pecuniary externalities. The evidence indicates that MaPs meaningfully shift corporate credit conditions and firms' leverage and investment, with especially pronounced effects for SMEs and bank-dependent firms. We synthesise results across bank-side instruments that operate through intermediaries' balance sheets and borrower-based underwriting limits, and discuss how credit reallocation across intermediaries and across countries shapes corporate outcomes. We also review evidence on interactions between MaPs and monetary policy, highlighting the importance of the joint policy mix for corporate credit conditions. We conclude with policy implications and a future research agenda.

title: AI, Capital, and Constraints
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: AI, Capital, and Constraints
detail.abstract:
Well-capitalized firms are undertaking a rapid and large expansion of artificial intelligence infrastructure capacity. This note examines that investment as a capital deployment problem, not as a potential indicator of the near-term value of the resulting AI deployment.

AI attracts capital not simply because of expected returns, but because a widely internalized narrative creates institutional pressure and a positive feedback loop: visible commitment to AI raises valuations, higher valuations increase the cost of underexposure, and capital is pulled forward to secure position rather than to clear on price. This dynamic concentrates investment into a narrow set of AI-linked assets and projects, committing demand rapidly and at scale for AI-linked infrastructure and the specialized inputs required to build it. That demand, however, is met by input-producing systems—power infrastructure, transport logistics, and advanced semiconductors—that are capacity-constrained and expand only on long industrial timelines that capital cannot materially compress.

When demand is committed ahead of capacity, price ceases to function as an effective coordinating signal. Rising costs do not defer demand or unlock proportional new supply, and allocation shifts away from price clearing toward queue position, permitting sequences, and access to manufacturing slots. In this environment, mispricing resolves through compressed investment returns, even if the underlying technology ultimately succeeds.

title: Reaching for Yield in Turbulent Times: Bank Liquidity Creation under Geopolitical Risk
affiliations: , Fordham University  , The University of Sydney - Discipline of Finance and The University of Sydney - Discipline of Finance

detail.title: Reaching for Yield in Turbulent Times: Bank Liquidity Creation under Geopolitical Risk
detail.abstract: Using a panel of commercial banks from 40 countries between 2001 and 2023, we find that heightened geopolitical risk (GPR) markedly increases bank liquidity creation. Exploiting the 2022 Russia-Ukraine war as a quasi-natural experiment, we identify this effect through a difference-indifferences framework that leverages both geographic exposure and trade linkages with the conflict region. The increase in liquidity creation is primarily profit-driven: banks expand lending, reduce cash holdings, and earn higher interest margins and returns during periods of elevated geopolitical tension. We find little evidence for alternative explanations, such as government intervention, precautionary borrowing, or monetary easing. The effect is more pronounced among larger, more profitable banks in competitive banking systems, but weakens during banking crises. Our findings highlight the strategic supply-side role of banks in responding to geopolitical risk, positioning GPR as a key external driver of financial intermediation.

title: Firm-Level Microsimulation of Intertemporal Corporate Tax Effects

detail.title: Firm-Level Microsimulation of Intertemporal Corporate Tax Effects
detail.abstract: This paper develops a general-purpose firm-level microsimulation model to analyse corporate tax systems and the intertemporal mechanisms of major tax base regulations. The model combines a stochastic forecasting component with a detailed and modular simulation of corporate tax rules. Firm-level profitability is projected using an autoregressive Monte Carlo approach, generating distributions of future pre-tax outcomes. These projections are translated into taxable income and corporate tax liability through the explicit modelling of tax depreciation regimes, investment incentives, earnings stripping rules, notional interest deductions on equity, and intertemporal loss offsetting. The model tracks the formation and utilisation of carryforwards at the firm level, thereby capturing non-linear, state-dependent, and path-dependent interactions between tax provisions over time. Designed to balance institutional realism, data availability, and flexibility, the model can be applied consistently across jurisdictions and reform scenarios. It provides a transparent tool for analysing mechanical revenue effects, firm-level tax burden distributions, and the sensitivity of outcomes to alternative corporate tax system designs.

title: It's About Time: Social Housing, Parental Labour Supply, and Long-term Child Outcomes
affiliations: University of British Columbia (UBC)

detail.title: It's About Time: Social Housing, Parental Labour Supply, and Long-term Child Outcomes
detail.abstract: I assess the effect of highly subsidized social housing on both parents' labour market outcomes and children's long-term earnings and educational attainment. I document substantial reductions in parents' labour supply and earnings around program entry, with nearly no effect on net-of-housing-cost income. A simple time-allocation model, in which social-housing receipt both relaxes the budget constraint and insures parents against earnings risk, rationalizes these large labour-supply responses. Then, I exploit variation in the timing of entry and find that children with longer exposure to social housing achieve better adult outcomes. I demonstrate that increases in parental time are a key causal factor in improvements in child outcomes. These results highlight a previously undocumented critical trade-off between maximizing the return for children and parents' labour market participation.

title: The Eternal Prompt: Lessons from Scripture, Talmud, and AI on the Primacy of the Question
affiliations: City University of New York (CUNY) - Koppelman School of Business

detail.title: The Eternal Prompt: Lessons from Scripture, Talmud, and AI on the Primacy of the Question
detail.abstract: The rise of large language models has renewed attention to a perennial insight: the quality of knowledge is inseparable from the quality of the questions that generate it. This paper argues that modern prompt engineering, the practice of crafting purposeful inquiries to elicit meaningful AI responses, reflects an ancient intellectual tradition deeply embedded in Jewish thought. Drawing on the Hebrew Bible and Talmud, this study demonstrates that foundational Jewish texts treat questioning as an epistemological imperative. Case studies include Abraham's challenge in Genesis, the dialogic structure of Job, the Four Children of the Haggadah, the Oven of Akhnai, and the schools of Hillel and Shammai. These are situated alongside modern scientific shifts from Newton and Einstein to Kahneman and Tversky, where progress originated in reframing questions rather than accumulating answers. Together, these sources suggest that genuine understanding comes from the discipline and humility to ask the right questions. AI does not render this ancient wisdom obsolete; it makes it uniquely visible and urgently relevant.

detail.abstract: We observe the simultaneous coexistence of legal de-globalization and illegal globalization. These two phenomena constitute the two major “sectors” that make up contemporary confrontational globalization. Illegal globalization is inherently more persistent, while legal de-globalization can be reversed through political decision-making.

title: Criminal Governance in Times of Crisis: Evidence from the COVID-19 Outbreak in Rio de Janeiro
affiliations: University of Chicago - Department of Political Science, Universidad EAFIT and Brazilian School of Public and Business Administration at the Getulio Vargas Foundation

detail.title: Criminal Governance in Times of Crisis: Evidence from the COVID-19 Outbreak in Rio de Janeiro
detail.abstract: In urban peripheries worldwide, and especially in Latin America, criminal groups use coercive power to impose rules on and provide order to civilians. The reasons why gangs govern in particular ways, or at all, are poorly understood. Many charge taxes in exchange for governance provision-suggesting they act as stationary banditsbut some do not. Many control retail drug markets, but some also earn rents from licit goods and services like cooking gas and internet. During the COVID-19 crisis, anecdotes of gangs enforcing lockdowns and providing health-related public goods suggested they seized opportunities to consolidate their authority and perceived legitimacy. We present novel, systematic data on criminal governance practices in Rio de Janeiro, whose gangs are notoriously militarized, persistent, and-usefully, from our perspective-diverse. While many belong to prison-based drug syndicates, others are police-linked groups known as milícias. We surveyed residents from almost 200 favelas about local gangs' type, economic and governance activities, taxation, and pandemic response. Contrary to expectations, we find that drug gangs and milícias alike earn rents from a range of licit products and services, enjoy similarly high levels of perceived legitimacy, and largely avoided involvement in pandemic response. Yet milicias are far more likely to tax, and seldom sell drugs. Our findings suggest that gangs' core motives are economic rather than political, that they strategically distinguish between direct taxation and extracting monopoly rents from control over utilities.

title: Consent Absent Consensus: A Principles-Based Framework for Institutional Sexual Consent Policies
affiliations: University of Arizona - James E. Rogers College of Law

detail.title: Consent Absent Consensus: A Principles-Based Framework for Institutional Sexual Consent Policies

publicationDetails.detailsText: Arizona Legal Studies Discussion Paper No. 26-2; 128 W. Va. L. Rev. 557 (2026)
publicationDetails.journalName: University of Arizona James E. Rogers College of Law Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Title IX requires educational institutions to address sexual misconduct but provides no clear standard for defining consent. In the absence of federal guidance, colleges and universities operate in a regulatory vacuum, producing inconsistent definitions, legal uncertainty, and contested understandings of what consent requires. Without a structured framework, institutions struggle to balance survivor protection, due process, and practical implementation.

This Article introduces a principles-based framework that supports clearer, more coherent consent policies. It identifies three interdependent elements of valid sexual consent: (1) Respect for Choices and Autonomy, which requires voluntary agreement free from coercion or pressure; (2) Informed Expectations and Transparency, which addresses the role of material disclosures in shaping sexual decisions; and (3) Capacity for Meaningful Participation, which focuses on the ability to understand, evaluate, and communicate consent, especially in contexts involving intoxication or cognitive impairment. Rather than prescribing uniform policies, this framework provides legal academics and college administrators with an analytical tool for evaluating existing definitions, identifying normative gaps, and building more coherent standards that reflect both ethical commitments and institutional realities.

In addition to articulating the framework, this Article offers a method for evaluating existing policies and testing the consequences of definitional variation. Through comparative policy analysis, hypothetical scenario application, and a three-part typology—Expansive, Intermediate, and Minimalist—this Article demonstrates how different evidentiary thresholds and normative priorities shape institutional outcomes. It shows how the principles frequently intersect and sometimes conflict, requiring adjudicators and policymakers to make value-based tradeoffs in design and implementation.

By combining normative clarity with institutional pragmatism, this Article offers legal academics and college policymakers a scalable model for building consent standards that reflect both ethical commitments and regulatory realities. The framework is not prescriptive, but adaptable—designed to help institutions clarify their definitions, train adjudicators, and better align policy with the lived complexity of campus sexual encounters.

title: Legal Contests, Compliance, and Collaboration with Artificial Intelligence
affiliations: Cornell University - Law School and The University of Texas at Dallas

detail.title: Legal Contests, Compliance, and Collaboration with Artificial Intelligence

detail.abstract: How will artificial intelligence reshape the legal system? Will it reduce the demand for human lawyers, or increase it by raising the returns to effort? Will it advantage plaintiffs or defendants-and under what conditions? Observers speculate on these questions, but the debate lacks grounding. We develop a simple family of models in which AI scales the conversion of human effort into verifiable legal evidence across three settings: contests, compliance, and collaboration. In adversarial contests before unbiased courts, AI complements human effort: both sides invest more, and litigation produces information that better tracks underlying merits. By contrast, in defense-biased settings, AI generates deterrence dynamics that reduce plaintiff effort and eventually deaden defense effort as well, diminishing information production. For compliance, whether AI substitutes or complements human labor depends on institutional design: outcome-based monitoring raises effort, while effort-based thresholds displace it. In collaborative legal contexts approximating transactional practice, human effort increases in equilibrium. A final extension examines hallucination, in which AI may generate forged material: hallucination weakens the link between effort and observed records in litigation but creates scope for doctrinal intervention through liability and evidentiary sanctions. Overall, AI's effects are mediated by institutional and doctrinal choices, shaping how technological change enters the legal system.

detail.abstract: This article examines the implementation of Anticipatory Artificial Intelligence (AI) Governance within the Provincial Council of Gipuzkoa (Basque Country) through an action research project designed to inform a Digital Inclusion Strategy led by the General Directorate for Human Rights and Democratic Culture (Presidency). Situating the study within debates on anticipatory governance, the article addresses the following research question: how can city-regional governments operationalize anticipatory AI governance to advance territorial digital inclusion while safeguarding democratic accountability and human digital rights? The project moves beyond industrial and productivity-centered approaches to AI, focusing instead on its ethical, socioeconomic , and territorial implications for citizens. The action research follows an eight-step methodological roadmap driven by Science for Policy approach (2024-2026): (i) alignment with the II Diversity Plan; (ii) the UIK International Summer School on Digital Inclusion & Generative AI (https://www.uik.eus/en/activity/digital-inclusiongenerative-artificial-intelligence-gipuzkoa-socially-cohesive-digitally); (iii) collaboration with six NGOs (Aniztasunaren Sarea) to establish a Digital Inclusion & Generative AI Decalogue; (iv) dissemination via local media; (v) academic engagement through Discover Cities (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44327-025-00116-9) and ICA2025 (https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/11352770); (vi) fieldwork across seven governmental departments; (vii) engagement with 11 municipalities through ElkarBizi intermunicipal network; and (viii) international dissemination at AAG2026 (https://aag-meetings.secureplatform.com/aag2026/gallery/rounds/149/details/87672). Methodologically, the project integrates a triangulated design structured around Science for Policy through (i) Knowledge Exchange, (ii) Stakeholder Engagement, and (iii) Open-Science Dissemination. Findings indicate that embedding anticipatory AI governance within territorial inclusion strategies strengthens policy foresight, enhances ethical reflexivity in algorithmic decision-making, and consolidates public trust. The Gipuzkoa model offers a replicable framework for territorial AI governance grounded in inclusion, transparency, and democratic innovation.

title: Welfare Retrenchment and Social Unrest

detail.title: Welfare Retrenchment and Social Unrest
detail.abstract: Does welfare retrenchment cause social unrest? I study this question by using parish-level expenditure on poor relief from post-Napoleonic England and applying generative AI to a corpus of 3.9 million newspaper column transcriptions to collect the category, date and location for each reported unrest incident. Reduced-form analysis leveraging a shift-share instrument finds a causal effect of welfare retrenchment on social unrest between 1819 and 1831, attributable to grievances arising from social and habitual comparisons. Simulations from a counterfactual analysis assuming blanket increases in welfare expenditure highlight the significance of social welfare provision in preventing large-scale unrest.

title: Beyond Penalties: Tax Shaming, Fiscal Transparency, and the Architecture of Global Tax Governance
affiliations: University of Coimbra Institute for Legal Research

detail.title: Beyond Penalties: Tax Shaming, Fiscal Transparency, and the Architecture of Global Tax Governance
detail.abstract: This study examines the use of tax shaming as a reputational enforcement tool in modern tax systems. It evaluates whether public disclosure of tax non-compliance can strengthen fiscal transparency and promote voluntary compliance without infringing on rights such as privacy and due process. Drawing on regulatory theory and crosscountry comparisons-including the UK, Nordic countries, the EU, Australia, the United States, Brazil, and Spain-the analysis identifies key principles of legitimacy, proportionality, and fairness that should guide its application. The study concludes by proposing a balanced framework to ensure that reputational enforcement supports effective and trustworthy tax governance.

title: Value of Grazing in Moroccan Forests at the Time of the Protectorate
affiliations: The Economist

detail.title: Value of Grazing in Moroccan Forests at the Time of the Protectorate

declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: Data from surveys conducted in the early 1930s were used to estimate the total value of grazing land and the revenue shortfall in the state budget due to the failure of the access tariff reform. The value of grazing land in the area under the French protectorate turned out to be of the same order of magnitude as the value of timber and non-timber forest products, or even higher, given the price distortions. The value thus calculated was appropriated primarily by users whose access to grazing land was almost free and whose livestock flocked to the forests exceeded their grazing capacity. If the initially planned tax reform had been implemented and the regulations governing grazing rights had been applied without compromise, the state could have had some leeway to capture a portion of this transfer and, at the same time, reduce the pressure that livestock exert on grazing lands and protect itself against the resulting risk of soil and environmental degradation. Estimates are made for the area of the Spanish sub-protectorate by transposing the unit values for the grazing of the French sub-protectorate, due to a lack of specific data on the state forests in this area.

title: Time Varying Skill: Analyzing Calstrs And An Internal GTAA Program, And 38 Us Public (And 3 Canadian) Pension Plans
affiliations: Georgetown University - McDonough School of Business

detail.title: Time Varying Skill: Analyzing Calstrs And An Internal GTAA Program, And 38 Us Public (And 3 Canadian) Pension Plans
detail.abstract:
Evaluating asset managers hired or being considered is a continuous, multi-period process. This paper develops a time-varying measure of skill (TVS), using the Muralidhar-U adaptation of Ambarish-Seigel skill equation, updating confidence in skill calculations as new performance data arrives. We apply the TVS framework to two distinct case studies: CalSTRS, using annual total fund data (1999–2023), and VIMCO’s internal GTAA program, using higher-frequency monthly data (2/2014–2/2026). The contrasting mandates and data frequencies highlight the flexibility and dynamic insights of the TVS methodology.

We also apply this technique to a unique data set of 38 US public 3 Canadian pension plans, for which we have varying lengths of track records. The results show interesting trends – some funds have steady TVS with high skill (Montgomery County and KPERS); some of the California funds in this sample have less than ideal TVS; some funds have shown a dramatic improvement in confidence in skill (like SWIB and MD SRA); and others are laggards (TX TRS, IL IMRF and CalPERS). A bit controversially, two results stand out: (i) the Canadian funds are clear outliers (for interesting reasons) and (ii) many award-winning CIOs have not demonstrated significant confidence that they are/were skillful.

TVS provides useful information for fiduciaries as diverse as Boards and CIOs of pension funds/endowments or heads of asset management companies to either maintain good processes and investment practices (high and rising TVS), or focus on fixing what appears to be ineffective (low and declining TVS).

title: Systems Analysis of Decision-Making under Ambiguity with Comparative Out-of-Sample Experimental Study of Geometric Dispersion Theory & Cumulative Prospect Theory
affiliations: Case Western Reserve University - School of Engineering and Case Western Reserve University - Case Western Reserve University, Computer Science

detail.title: Systems Analysis of Decision-Making under Ambiguity with Comparative Out-of-Sample Experimental Study of Geometric Dispersion Theory & Cumulative Prospect Theory

declarations.ethicsApproval: This work involved human subjects in its research. The authors confirm that all human subject research procedures and protocols are exempt from review board approval.

detail.abstract: 1-In this paper, we develop a new descriptive model for ambiguity decision-making called Ambiguity Geometric Dispersion Theory (A-GDT). In out-of-sample predictions, we find that A-GDT is experimentally superior to all models which it generalizes; specifically, cumulative prospect theory (CPT), subjective expected utility (SEU), alpha-maxmin expected utility (α-MEU), vector expected utility (VEU), and expected utility theory (EUT). We ran an experimental study of 150 decisions under ambiguity by 310 subjects by operationalizing payoffs, probability, and ambiguity. We show that subjects exhibit behavior that contradicts many decision models, such as CPT, SEU, α-MEU, and EUT; but not A-GDT. In out-of-sample studies with the same number of parameters, the A-GDT model predicts both representative (aggregate) agent and individual preferences substantially better than other well-known ambiguity models. Specifically, a three-parameter A-GDT is substantially superior to CPT and all other important models. Furthermore, significance testing in a paired comparison of models shows that subjects' behavior matches the A-GDT model markedly better than other models. A new rate-of-degradation analysis demonstrates that A-GDT's predictions are far more stable than other models as the insample size is decreased. In addition, the A-GDT model not only can resolve typical Ellsberg-like behavior, but it can also resolve hypothetical and real-life ambiguity problems with multiple sources of ambiguity including the paradoxes by Machina.

title: Online Supplement for: Systems Analysis of Game Geometric Dispersion for Generalizing the Nash Equilibrium and a Comparative Out-of-Sample Empirical Study
affiliations: Case Western Reserve University - School of Engineering and Case Western Reserve University - Case Western Reserve University, Computer Science

detail.title: Online Supplement for: Systems Analysis of Game Geometric Dispersion for Generalizing the Nash Equilibrium and a Comparative Out-of-Sample Empirical Study

contentFormat.other: Online supplement for a working paper contain details of implementation and data

detail.abstract: Introducing payoff asymmetry in classical games has been shown to cause large inconsistencies between experimental behavior and theoretical predictions of the Nash Equilibrium, which cannot be explained with error and noise. In this paper, we propose the game geometric dispersion (G-GD) model which generalizes Nash as well as the widely studied linear models of other-regarding preferences in games.  By introducing nonlinearity into the player’s utility, G-GD allows the equilibrium to shift with changes in players’ own payoffs. Drawing on extensive experimental evidence from the literature, we show that G-GD generates equilibrium outcomes more consistent with observed behavior than both Nash Equilibrium and prevailing other-regarding models, whether linear or non-linear. Unlike models with significant assumption of error and noise, G-GD retains simplicity and behavioral justifications. Using comparative empirical analysis of five game theory models, we demonstrate that G-GD offers a flexible, behaviorally grounded, and theoretically sound approach for understanding game theoretic strategic interactions, bridging the gap between theoretical predictions and experimental evidence. The model comparisons are validated by out-of-sample statistical analysis.

title: Greenwashing or Pragmatism?
affiliations: University of Warwick - Department of Economics, Ivy College of Business, Iowa State University and

detail.title: Greenwashing or Pragmatism?
detail.abstract: Shareholder support for environmental and social (ES) proposals increased by more than 50% between 2010 and 2020, yet the content of such proposals can vary substantially. We first document that there has been a large retreat in big-ask proposals (e.g., demanding operational changes for firms). The big-ask proposals fell from about 40% of ES ballots to roughly 5%, being replaced by small-ask proposals (e.g., requesting additional disclosure), and the increase in overall support rate is driven by favorable votes on small asks compared to big asks. However, we caution against interpreting these trends as greenwashing. Investigating both sides of shareholder democracy (proponents and voters), we develop and estimate a structural model in which ES proponents choose a portfolio of proposal types, anticipating vote outcomes. The model captures a feedback: changes in voting reshape the mix of sponsored proposals, and that mix, in turn, shapes observed support rates. Counterfactuals based on resubmission-style benchmarks suggest that the early part of the decade featured an oversupply of big-ask proposals and a moderate undersupply of small-ask proposals; the subsequent decline in big asks reflects an equilibrium correction toward small asks that are expected to receive meaningful support to generate incremental progress in ES. Therefore, the correction, along with growing voter support, suggests a shift towards a more pragmatic approach to ES issues rather than greenwashing.

title: Connectedness of Inflation Expectations, Prices, and Real Economic Activity: Evidence from Pakistan
affiliations: State Bank of Pakistan and State Bank of Pakistan

detail.title: Connectedness of Inflation Expectations, Prices, and Real Economic Activity: Evidence from Pakistan
detail.abstract: This study analyzes how inflation expectations influence Pakistan's inflation dynamics through spillover transmission among key macroeconomic variables using monthly data from January 2012 to June 2025. The framework combines household inflation expectations with headline inflation, economic policy uncertainty, the exchange rate, oil prices, lending rates, and industrial activity. To Uncover heterogenous transmission channels, headline inflation is further decomposed into food, energy, and core components. Using a time-varying parameter VAR with frequency-domain connectedness decomposition, the results show that economic policy uncertainty is the dominant source of shocks, while inflation expectations function as net transmitters of volatility, in contrast to realized inflation, which primarily absorbs disturbances. Disaggregated evidence shows that expectation-driven spillovers propagate most strongly through food and energy prices and then pass through indirectly to core inflation. Overall, the findings underscore the central role of expectations and uncertainty in Pakistan's inflation dynamics. The results highlight the importance of anchoring inflation expectations, strengthening fiscalmonetary coordination, and managing policy uncertainty as central elements of macroeconomic stabilization.

title: The Impact Mechanism of Industrial Spatial Agglomeration on Carbon Emission Intensity in Chinese Urban Agglomerations
affiliations: Jilin University of Finance and Economics, Jilin University of Finance and Economics, Jilin University of Finance and Economics, Jilin University of Finance and Economics, Jilin University of Finance and Economics, Jilin University of Finance and Economics and Jilin University of Finance and Economics

detail.title: The Impact Mechanism of Industrial Spatial Agglomeration on Carbon Emission Intensity in Chinese Urban Agglomerations
detail.abstract: Clarifying the characteristics of industrial spatial agglomeration within urban agglomerations and the associated impact mechanism on carbon emission intensity is crucial for formulating regional collaborative carbon reduction strategies. Focusing on China’s 18 major urban agglomerations and employing methods such as the location quotient (LQ) index and the spatial Durbin model (SDM), this study analyzes the features of industrial spatial agglomeration and the influence of that agglomeration on carbon emission intensity, from 2002 to 2023. The key findings are: (1) Industrial spatial agglomeration in Chinese urban agglomerations is pronounced, with the pattern of spatial agglomeration gradually shifting from single-point concentration to clustered agglomeration. (2) While total carbon emissions (TCE) and per capita carbon emissions (PCCE) in these regions increased significantly, carbon emission intensity per unit output exhibited a continuous declining trend. Regions with higher carbon emission intensity showed a tendency to shift towards urban agglomerations in northern China. (3) An analysis of core explanatory variables reveals the multifaceted impact of industrial agglomeration on carbon emission intensity. Specialized industrial agglomeration (SIA) reduces emission intensity through technology spillovers, but SIA is accompanied by rebound effects and carbon transfer to neighboring areas. Technology-intensive agglomeration (TIA) increases local emission intensity while decreasing TCE and PCCE. However, TIA also faces challenges in reducing emission intensity and issues of spatial spillover. An analysis of control variables identifies technological innovation as the core driver for reducing carbon emissions. (4) Based on these findings, carbon reduction strategies tailored to the industrial spatial agglomeration processes in urban agglomerations are proposed.

title: When Copyright Becomes Credit Risk: Artificial Intelligence and Intangible Asset Financing

detail.title: When Copyright Becomes Credit Risk: Artificial Intelligence and Intangible Asset Financing
detail.abstract: Discussions on the impact of artificial intelligence on copyright law have largely focused on infringement, fair use, authorship and the permissibility of training models on protected works. These debates often unfold at the level of doctrine or ex post liability. However, the rapid growth of intangible asset financing requires a shift in perspective. As intellectual property is increasingly used as collateral and securitized in financial transactions, copyright uncertainty assumes new commercial significance at the pre-transaction stage. What has received far less attention is how copyright uncertainty, particularly in AI-mediated assets, filters into pre-transaction due diligence. This uncertainty gets commercially sensitive, especially where intellectual property is relied upon as collateral or is the subject of securitization. In such context, copyright infringement is not merely a legal concern, it becomes a determinant of valuation, bankability, and credit risk. As AI systems increasingly rely on data-intensive architectures, copyright questions are migrating from the margins of enforcement into the core of transactional risk assessment. Historically, copyright law occupied a relatively modest place in transactional due diligence when compared to patents or registered rights. While ownership and chain of title have always mattered, infringement risk was often treated as contingent, arising from specific uses rather than from the existence of the asset itself. A software programme for instance cannot be a topic of copyright infringement for existing, unless it has been used in a way not authorized. In most cases, copyright risk could be managed operationally, usually through licensing, takedown procedures or adjustments to modes of exploitation. As a result, copyright rarely threatened the fundamental financeability of an asset. However, the operation of AI destabilizes this assumption. The infringement question may arise now from the model's formation rather than its deployment. This is to say that infringement risk becomes inherent in the model's formation, making it difficult to predict or control when protected expression may be reproduced, thereby placing copyrighted works at risk of unauthorized use. Where an AI-system is trained without authorization and its generated outputs serve as functional substitutes in the consumption market, they introduce uncertainty into the original asset's future revenue stream. The question now is whether the original asset's economic value can still be said to subsist. Can the streaming revenue remain substantial enough to stand as collateral for financial arrangement? This paper demonstrates how copyright infringement by artificial intelligence reduces the economic reliability of intellectual property for purposes of collateralization, securitization, and sale-and-lease-back structures. Likewise, it clarifies what differences obtain between AI-driven companies and right holders, and what financial implication the infringement has on both of them. Furthermore, the paper demonstrates how the IP-backed financial structures work with copyright. Finally, it looks into the effects of the infringement on copyright and what pre-transaction due diligence will be like for investors and financiers.

title: The Iron Rice Bowl Revival: Why Public Sector Jobs Outpay Private Enterprises for Fresh Graduates in China
affiliations: Hanshan Normal University and Hanshan Normal University

detail.title: The Iron Rice Bowl Revival: Why Public Sector Jobs Outpay Private Enterprises for Fresh Graduates in China
detail.abstract: Challenging the conventional wisdom that private sector jobs pay more, this study documents an "Iron Rice Bowl Revival"—a phenomenon where public sector starting salaries significantly exceed private sector wages for fresh graduates from non-elite universities in China. Analyzing administrative data from 2,053 mathematics graduates (2020–2025) at a Guangdong normal university, we find public sector employees earn 914 CNY (18.1%) more monthly than private sector counterparts (t=8.81, p<.001). This premium intensified dramatically after 2023, from 5.5% to 27.9%, coinciding with China's "civil service examination fever." Propensity score analysis yields a robust average treatment effect of +565 CNY. Including non-wage benefits, the total compensation gap reaches 25–35%. These findings reframe "civil service fever" as rational economic behavior, with implications for labor market theory and graduate career counseling in transitional economies.

detail.abstract: Objective: To examine the relationship between psychological safety in clinical learning environments and learning engagement and clinical self-efficacy among undergraduate nursing students. Methodology: A descriptive cross-sectional study was conducted among 500 Level 3 and Level 4 nursing students enrolled in private nursing schools in Region I, Philippines. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire assessing psychological safety in clinical placements, learning engagement, and clinical selfefficacy. Internal consistency was evaluated using Cronbach's alpha. Descriptive statistics summarized participant characteristics and scale distributions. Spearman correlation and multiple linear regression analyses were performed to examine associations among the variables. Results: Participants reported moderate levels of psychological safety (3.02 ± 1.28), learning engagement (2.99 ± 1.25), and clinical self-efficacy (3.00 ± 1.27). All scales demonstrated excellent internal consistency (α = 0.968-0.975). Psychological safety was positively associated with learning engagement (r = 0.527, p < 0.001) and clinical self-efficacy (r = 0.628, p < 0.001). Regression analysis indicated that psychological safety significantly predicted learning engagement (B = 0.518, p < 0.001). Both psychological safety (B = 0.388, p < 0.001) and learning engagement (B = 0.456, p < 0.001) independently predicted clinical selfefficacy. Conclusion: Perceived psychological safety in clinical settings is strongly related to student engagement and confidence in clinical performance. Educational strategies that cultivate respectful supervision and open communication may strengthen professional preparation and support readiness for practice.

title: Welfare-maximizing Budget-balanced Mechanisms for Public Goods

detail.title: Welfare-maximizing Budget-balanced Mechanisms for Public Goods
detail.abstract: We study deterministic direct mechanisms for the provision of an indivisible public good with private values and known type distributions. Imposing dominant-strategy incentive compatibility, ex post individual rationality, and exact ex post budget balance, welfare maximization reduces to choosing provision thresholds (cost shares) that sum to the cost (the "Third Best" class characterized by Kuzmics and Steg). Exact ex post balance adds an individual-feasibility bottleneck: provision requires that every agent can cover her assigned share. Using a reliability-theory representation in terms of survival, hazard, and mean residual life functions, we characterize when equal cost shares (symmetric thresholds) are optimal in the i.i.d. symmetric environment. For two agents (N = 2), symmetry is optimal if and only if the ratio of mean residual life to hazard is decreasing; symmetry is optimal for all N ≥ 2 if and only if the survival function is log-concave (equivalently, the hazard rate is increasing). We then compare Third-Best welfare to the VCG/pivot benchmark. When costs scale proportionally with population size, we derive the exponential rate of the welfare gap via large-deviation methods, separating an individual "everyone can pay" tail event from the aggregate feasibility event. In heterogeneous environments with independent types and log-concave survivals, we establish a convex formulation and provide KKT characterizations. Finally, numerical illustrations quantify how limited deficit tolerance (a relaxation of exact budget balance) can recover substantial welfare.

title: Domestic Market Segmentation and Spatial Income Inequality
affiliations: Miami University and University of Houston

detail.title: Domestic Market Segmentation and Spatial Income Inequality
detail.abstract: In this paper, we study spatial income inequality within China. Using unique interregional trade data, we document a significant negative provincial border effect: in the industrial sector, trade between two cities in different provinces is about 92% lower than trade between cities within the same province, suggesting the presence of strong domestic market segmentation. To quantify these effects, we develop and calibrate a multi-region, multi-sector quantitative general equilibrium model that features provincial trade frictions. Counterfactuals show that removing provincial trade frictions reduces variance of log real wages by about 8% and lowers the 90/10 income ratio by about 17%.

title: The Cantor's Paradise
affiliations: Artificial Intelligence in Finance Institute

detail.title: The Cantor's Paradise
detail.abstract: Georg Cantor (1845-1918) transformed infinity from a philosophical notion into a precise mathematical structure. His key insight-that two sets have the same size exactly when their elements can be placed in bijection-led to a rigorous theory of cardinality revealing an unexpected hierarchy of infinite magnitudes. This survey develops the full Cantorian programme with detailed proofs and modern context. We establish that |Z| = |Q| = ℵ 0 , build a countability toolkit (closure under countable unions, countability of algebraic numbers, existence of transcendentals), and present Cantor's diagonal argument to show |R| > ℵ 0. The Cantor-Bernstein-Schröder theorem yields |P(N)| = |R| and |R n | = |R|, while Cantor's power-set theorem |A| < |P(A)| generates an unbounded tower of cardinals motivating the aleph and beth hierarchies. We explain how naive set theory collapses under Russell's paradox and how Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory with Choice (ZFC) resolves it, developing the cumulative hierarchy V α , ordinal arithmetic, transfinite induction, and Cantor normal form. König's theorem and its corollaries constrain cardinal exponentiation. On the analytic side, we construct the Cantor set, establish its measure-zero yet uncountable character, and discuss Cantor space, the Cantor function, and Hausdorff dimension. The independence of the Continuum Hypothesis is treated via Gödel's constructible universe L and Cohen's forcing. We conclude by tracing Cantor's diagonal method through Gödel's incompleteness theorems, Turing's Halting Problem, and the modern large-cardinal hierarchy. We also address the recently strengthened evidence-including a long-lost 1873 letter discovered in 2025-that Cantor published key results from Richard Dedekind's correspondence without adequate attribution, and discuss its implications for the historiography of set theory.

title: The Original Defensive War Power

detail.title: The Original Defensive War Power
detail.abstract:
In justifying recent military actions lacking congressional authorization, presidents have invoked a "defensive" war power to justify everything from attacks on drug boats to air battles over Israel to the bombing of Iran's nuclear facilities. The Department of Justice Office of Legal Counsel (OLC) has enabled these operations through an expansive interpretation of the President's power to wage a defensive war. OLC grounds this expansive presidential authority in President Washington's 1790 offensive against the Wabash Indians and Jefferson's 1801 naval operations against Barbary pirates. This Article shows that OLC has fundamentally misread both episodes, and that a third largely ignored conflict provides further confirmation of a restrictive unilateral presidential war power.
Examining contemporaneous debates in all three conflicts—the Northwestern Confederacy War, the First Barbary War, and Andrew Jackson's 1818 seizure of East Florida—this article recovers a narrower original understanding of the defensive war power. The original doctrine only authorized the President to (1) repel an actual invasion; or (2) fight a war already declared against the United States by a foreign power. OLC’s interpretation is not a faithful application of Founding-era precedents, but an adaptation to social, technological, and geopolitical changes that have lowered the political and practical costs of unilateral action. This Article closes by considering the implications of the original defensive war power for interbranch cooperation on judicial review in national security matters.

detail.abstract: This paper explores whether the U.S. Defend Trade Secrets Act (DTSA) increased the declaration of trade secrets. Leveraging cross-sectoral variation in the importance of trade secrets prior to the DTSA, empirical results show that the DTSA was followed by an increase in the intensive margin of trade secrets declaration in service industries, not in manufacturing industries though. The extensive margin of trade secret declaration increased in both services and manufacturing, where the surge was strongest in manufacturing. The extensive margin increased most strongly for manufacturing with a high sectoral R&D intensity. The results are of interest to policy makers as trade secrets can hinder knowledge flows with potential implications for innovation.

Do Treasury Bond Returns Affect the Stock Market Differently in Crisis and Non-crisis Conditions in Brazil? Evidence from a
Markov Switching Model
detail.abstract: The literature has documented a negative relationship between stock market performance and Treasury bond returns, or equivalently, interest rates. However, the magnitude of this relationship may differ between crisis and non-crisis conditions. This article aims to identify periods of crisis in the Brazilian stock market and to analyze how Treasury bond market returns affect stock market performance under both crisis and non-crisis conditions. The analysis covers the period from January 2002 to December 2024. Using a Markov switching model, we identify several crisis periods. In addition, we find an inverse relationship between Treasury bond market returns and stock market performance, with a stronger magnitude during crisis conditions. This article provides support for the formulation of effective investment strategies for capital protection during crises in Brazil, as such strategies reallocate capital toward Treasury bonds indexed to the Selic rate, which are commonly considered safe haven assets.

title: Coyote Lake and the Accommodation Doctrine in a Sea of Uncertainty
affiliations: Yale College

detail.title: Coyote Lake and the Accommodation Doctrine in a Sea of Uncertainty
detail.abstract: For more than half a century, the accommodation doctrine has quietly transformed from a narrow common-law safeguard against abuse into a significant check on the rights of the mineral owner. However, applying the accommodation doctrine consistently and appropriately is not a simple task. In this Note, I argue that the majority opinion in Coyote Lake v. City of Lubbock is partially responsible for this confusion, because not only does the majority appear to be at odds with the concurrence by Justice Boyd, the decision brushes by the property deed’s language, thus leaving it ambiguous how far the accommodation doctrine ought to reach. The result has been a methodological and legal confusion both about how the accommodation doctrine ought to apply and the breadth of its scope.

detail.abstract: This Article argues that the statutory elements required to state a claim under the Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act’s (“TVPRA”) forced labor statute equate to an enumeration of the definition of coercive-control-based domestic violence. Applied in conjunction with existing state court remedies, this framework can be used to maximize monetary damages for victims and supplement the collectability tools available, especially in high-net-worth New York matrimonial proceedings. Commentators have often limited their analysis to the intimacy of domestic violence, without exploring the financial constraints that prevent spouses from leaving, force the victims that do leave to absorb the compounding cost of exit and recovery, and fail to place victims in their rightful position had the harm not occurred. Essentially, this Article reframes the age-old question that plagues victims of domestic violence. Instead of asking why victims do not leave, it asks what leaving costs and identifies an additional mechanism by which that cost can be recovered.
