detail.abstract: The integration of Information Technology (IT) into agriculture holds significant potential for transforming traditional farming practices, enhancing productivity, and improving farmers' livelihoods. This study assessed the awareness and utilization of IT-driven agricultural technologies among farmers in Nigeria. A multi-stage sampling technique was used to select 384 farmers across three agricultural zones. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire and analyzed using descriptive statistics, correlation analysis. The results revealed a high level of awareness of basic technologies like mobile phones (95%) and radio/TV programs (82%), but low awareness of more advanced tools like drones (15%) and precision agriculture tools (12%). Major sources of information were radio/TV (78%), peers (65%), and mobile phone networks (60%), while extension agents (35%) and NGOs (28%) played a lesser role. Utilization was primarily for market access (70%) and financial transactions (via mobile money) (65%), but minimal for farm decisionsupport and precision tools. Socioeconomic factors such as age, education, income, and ICT literacy significantly influenced both awareness and utilization (p<0.01). Key constraints included poor network connectivity (90%), high cost of technology (85%), unstable power supply (80%), and low digital literacy (75%). Farmers who utilized IT tools perceived significant benefits in market access, income, and decision-making. The study recommends strengthening extension services through IT integration, subsidizing smart technologies, improving rural digital infrastructure, and implementing targeted digital literacy training programs to enhance adoption and effective utilization.

title: Political Impartiality and Professionalisation of Municipal Servants: European Experience for Post-war Ukraine

detail.title: Political Impartiality and Professionalisation of Municipal Servants: European Experience for Post-war Ukraine
detail.abstract:
Ukraine’s full-scale defence against Russian aggression coincides with its candidacy for EU membership and an ongoing decentralisation reform that places unprecedented responsibility on local self-government bodies. While municipalities have played a crucial role in territorial defence and civilian protection, the war has exposed systemic weaknesses in the political impartiality and professionalism of municipal civil servants, including collaborationism in occupied territories and pervasive political interference in personnel policy. Political bias within municipal service undermines public trust, fuels corruption, and generates direct risks for national security.

The article conceptualises political impartiality as the capacity of municipal servants to perform their duties independent of party affiliation, personal political views, or external pressure, and argues that this principle is inseparable from the broader professionalisation of municipal service. It provides a critical assessment of the new Law of Ukraine “On Service in Local Self-Government Bodies” No. 3077-IX, highlighting its potential to depoliticise local service through competitive recruitment, clear separation of political and administrative positions, performance evaluation, and continuous professional development, while also identifying key implementation risks such as financial constraints, lack of secondary legislation, and resistance from political elites. Drawing on the experience of Poland (KSAP), Germany (Berufsbeamtentum), and the Netherlands (“Public Sector Bargain”), as well as ReSPA programmes, the article formulates practical recommendations for establishing a politically neutral, professional municipal civil service tailored to Ukraine’s post-war reconstruction and accelerated European integration.

detail.abstract: Budish (2025) proves that the cost of Nakamoto blockchain trust scales linearly with value secured. I show this binds only where processing and trust are fused. I develop a two-sided payment platform model yielding four results: a cost-separation proposition extending Budish; comparative statics showing processing cost reductions propagate through equilibrium fees and adoption; a welfare result with two-sided amplification; and dissolution of natural monopoly under horizontal scaling. Calibrating with independently verified engineering data and public financial filings implies US welfare gains of $2.8-$21 billion annually from infrastructure cost reduction alone.

detail.abstract: Companies across industries seek to assess the costs of complying with environmental reg ulations and meeting voluntary emission targets. This paper develops a carbon abatement cost model for firms operating a portfolio of assets with differing cost or load profiles. The resulting abatement cost curves serve as a decision tool for configuring individual assets to achieve firm-wide emission reductions at least cost. We apply our model to urban bus fleets regulated under the California Cap-and-Trade Program. We find that a carbon price of $35 per ton of CO2e (2024 average) incentivizes firms to configure their fleets such that battery electric drivetrains constitute 70% of usable installed capacity and 92% of annual demand, while diesel drivetrains serve peak loads. Since the resulting emissions are fairly inelastic to the carbon price, we conclude that the life-cycle cost per mile would increase substantialy if deep decarbonization were to be induced entirely by higher carbon prices.

title: Sunk Capital and Repeated Interaction in Nakamoto Consensus: A Note on Budish (2025)
affiliations: University of Exeter

detail.title: Sunk Capital and Repeated Interaction in Nakamoto Consensus: A Note on Budish (2025)
detail.abstract: Budish [2025] shows that the flow cost of Nakamoto-style trust scales linearly with the value secured, relying on a one-shot, free-entry formulation in which interaction is memoryless. A process is formally memoryless if and only if future states are independent of history given the present. The Nakamoto protocol violates this property through two hardcoded temporal structures: a 100-block coinbase maturity rule and a 2,016block difficulty adjustment. Both make future payoffs explicitly history-dependent. Jointly with sunk capital and pseudonymity, these features introduce continuation values, asymmetric attack costs, and Beckerian deterrence-forces the model eliminates by construction. Appendix A documents fourteen such assumptions. The three analysed here are central to the model's application to proof-of-work systems as they exist.

title: The Too Few To Fail Traders In Modern Markets
affiliations: Vanderbilt University - Law School and University of Utah - David Eccles School of Business

detail.title: The Too Few To Fail Traders In Modern Markets

publicationDetails.journalName: Vanderbilt University Law School Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
In U.S. public equity markets, two trading firms – Citadel Securities and Virtu Financial – help execute around 70% of all retail orders. Citadel, by itself, intermediates 25% of all U.S. stock trades. Its rival, Jane Street, reports being involved in 2% of trading across 20 countries. Buying and selling in fractions of a second, a small cohort of firms including Citadel, Jane Street and Virtu, have come to dominate the business of making markets, offering themselves as trading counterparties for others. This function is critical for market quality and continuity – so much so that, until recently, it came with its dedicated body of laws and mandates, requiring those charged with making markets to promise to defend them in times of trouble. Today, it is more informally practiced, characterized by fierce competition for each trade, while becoming concentrated in the hands of a few repeat winners.

This Article highlights this phenomenon to offer three contributions. First, we show that today’s capital market structure is novel in allowing individual market makers to capture as much share as their success permits. This has resulted in the emergence of a handful of prolific traders becoming critical to market function and investor protection. Second, it analyzes this phenomenon to argue that it comes with both benefits and costs. Avoiding knee-jerk conclusions that these firms have become “too-big-to-fail” or excessively extractive for investors, concentration can, in fact, promote investment in long-term market quality to offset the dangers of a relatively informal and hyper-fast system of securities intermediation. But there are also serious risks. Even if a market-maker’s failure does not trigger catastrophic collapses, its loss can decimate the quality of the trading experience for investors and for trading to be capable of conveying reliable information in prices. Third, we propose two solutions to protect markets and investors from the costs of major market makers failing: (i) ex-ante, for top traders to prepare a living-will that maps out the impact of their intermediation and helps regulators understand what might happen if this becomes scarce; and (ii) ex-post, for these firms to fund a collective emergency facility that encourages them to keep trading during crises rather than exiting just because they can. This design helps to mitigate the risks for capital markets where intermediation is largely informal and dependent on a cohort of firms that are few in number but prolific in their impact.

title: AI in EU Law: Training, Hallucinations, Memorization, and the Core Regulatory Architecture
affiliations: European University Viadrina Frankfurt (Oder) - European New School of Digital Studies

detail.title: AI in EU Law: Training, Hallucinations, Memorization, and the Core Regulatory Architecture
detail.abstract: This chapter examines the regulatory architecture for artificial intelligence in European Union law across the three stages of the machine learning pipeline: training, model, and output. First, in the training context, it analyzes the tensions between GDPR requirements and large-scale AI training, the copyright framework under the CDSM Directive's text and data mining exceptions, and the AI Act's data governance obligations. I also offer a detailed assessment of the GDPR Omnibus proposals. Second, at the model level, the chapter discusses the divergent rulings in Getty Images v Stability AI and GEMA v OpenAI on the question whether trained models constitute reproductions of copyrighted works. It also weighs in on the structurally parallel question whether models themselves constitute personal data. At the output level, it addresses hallucinations under the accuracy principle and proposes a strict liability regime modeled on pharmaceutical law. The chapter identifies a structural symmetry between data protection and copyright: in both domains, legally protected content is encoded in model parameters in a manner that renders surgical excision technically near-infeasible. It argues, however, that the appropriate remedies diverge-property rules for data protection with specific exceptions, liability rules with outputbased remuneration for copyright. The chapter concludes with policy proposals for each level of the pipeline and advocates a regulatory approach that combines technology-neutral baseline protection with targeted technology-specific interventions.

title: Internal Migration and Interest Rate Pass-through to Deposits

detail.title: Internal Migration and Interest Rate Pass-through to Deposits
detail.abstract: Does internal migration reshape banks' deposit spreads and volumes by altering deposit market power? Using branch-and county-level U.S. data from 2001 to 2021, we construct bank-county measures of exposure to asymmetric migration flows. We find that immigration narrows spreads and increases deposit volumes, whereas emigration widens spreads and decreases volumes. These effects persist after controlling for local economic conditions and market concentration, indicating that migration introduces a competitive margin that operates independently of prevailing local structure. By changing depositor mobility across markets, migration modifies banks' ability to sustain spreads and thus the value of their deposit franchise. Our findings establish internal migration as a fundamental determinant of deposit market functioning and a key driver of cross-market heterogeneity in monetary policy transmission.

title: The Myth of the Zero-Sum: Rethinking Acculturation in American Politics

detail.title: The Myth of the Zero-Sum: Rethinking Acculturation in American Politics

detail.abstract: Acculturation theory has long assumed a zero-sum tradeoff where stronger attachment to a dominant culture means weaker attachment to a heritage culture. This foundational premise has never been empirically tested, yet it governs how political science measures and understands political incorporation. Using comparative cluster analysis across multiple algorithms with extensive validation procedures, this paper provides the first rigorous test of the binary model against a bidirectional alternative, drawing on the 2006 Latino National Survey (N = 4,785 eligible voters). The binary model fails. Four distinct acculturation orientations emergebicultural (68.4%), assimilationist (14.7%), culture-affirming (9.0%), and demicultural (7.9%)and hybrid orientations constitute over three-quarters of the sample. The zero-sum framework structurally excludes the majority it claims to explain. These findings challenge foundational assumptions about acculturation theory and political incorporation, and demonstrate how unsupervised machine learning with rigorous validation enables hypothesis testing of theoretical frameworks long treated as settled.

detail.abstract: Defined benefit (DB) pension plans are important to employee welfare. However, they carry risk as they are subject to minimum funding requirements. We examine the effect of a relaxation in pension funding rules on employee satisfaction by exploiting the adoption of the Moving Ahead for Progress in the 21st Century Act (MAP-21). We find that employees of DB firms are less satisfied with their firms and their senior managers, after MAP-21. However, this is evident only when there is also wealth transfer to shareholders (i.e., share repurchases) or to managers themselves (i.e., higher bonus compensation) instead of investments in capital or R&D. Furthermore, the documented negative MAP-21 effects are concentrated in firms where employee interests are most at risk, namely when DB plans are significantly underfunded. Overall, our results provide novel insights into how employees react to pension plans changes.

title: Stablecoin Cards and the Emergence of Blockchain Retail Payments
affiliations: Marquette University

detail.title: Stablecoin Cards and the Emergence of Blockchain Retail Payments
detail.abstract: Stablecoins, cryptocurrencies engineered to maintain a stable value relative to fiat currencies, have become one of the fastest-growing segments of the digital asset ecosystem. While early research focused primarily on their role in cryptocurrency trading and decentralized finance, stablecoins are increasingly being used for real-world payments. One of the most notable developments in this transition is the emergence of stablecoin-linked payment cards, which allow consumers to spend digital dollars at traditional merchants through established card networks such as Visa and Mastercard. This paper documents the rapid growth of stablecoin card spending and examines its implications for payment infrastructure, merchant economics, consumer fee structures, and regulatory policy. Drawing on data from Artemis Analytics, industry reporting, and payment network disclosures, the analysis shows that monthly crypto-card transaction volumes expanded from approximately $100 million in early 2023 to more than $1.5 billion by late 2025, reaching an annualized spending rate exceeding $18 billion. The paper also examines how stablecoin cards alter fee dynamics for merchants and consumers, how traditional card networks have responded to blockchain-based payment instruments, and what regulatory and competitive implications may follow from continued adoption. Although still modest relative to the global payments market, the rapid expansion of stablecoin card usage suggests that stablecoins may be transitioning from speculative trading instruments into a new form of digital payment infrastructure.

title: Analysts' Response to 'AI Washing' in Earnings Conference Calls
affiliations: , Bayes Business School, City University London and

detail.title: Analysts' Response to 'AI Washing' in Earnings Conference Calls
detail.abstract: Heightened investor attention on artificial intelligence (AI) raises the possibility that firms may opportunistically exaggerate their AI activities to influence market perceptions. We study earnings conference call disclosures that reference AI and utilise the launch of ChatGPT as an exogenous AI shock. We identify a subset of firms, termed 'Speculative firms', that issue speculative AI disclosures despite having made no observable AI-related investments. While, on average, analysts and investors do not differentiate between Speculative firms and those with concrete AI disclosure-evidenced by comparable revisions to target prices and stock price performance-we show that analyst experience plays a critical moderating role. More experienced analysts systematically assign lower target prices to Speculative firms, consistent with a more discerning interpretation of technologically ambiguous narratives. We do not find that speculative firms benefit from (i) greater inclusion in AI ETFs, (ii) increased analyst coverage, (iii) higher trading volume, or experience (i) higher analyst processing costs or (ii) higher capex intensity. Collectively, these results provide novel evidence on heterogeneity in analyst responses to AI-related disclosures and shed light on the capital market consequences of AI washing practices.

title: Older Households are Moving Closer to their Adult Children: Implications for Urban Planning and Housing Policy

detail.title: Older Households are Moving Closer to their Adult Children: Implications for Urban Planning and Housing Policy
detail.abstract: This paper explores the mobility and residential choices of older adults, focusing on how the location of adult children influences these outcomes. Using the geocoded Health and Retirement Study, we undertake a descriptive analysis of older households' migration patterns and subsequent residential experiences. We find that moving significantly increases the likelihood of living closer to adult children and grandchildren, as well as receiving in-kind assistance from a child, and providing care to a grandchild. Furthermore, households who move closer to adult children are more likely to settle in high density zip codes and large metropolitan areas-locations that tend to offer more aging-friendly amenities. These findings have important policy implications for local housing supply regulation, and the provision of local services and infrastructure that can support older adults with aging-appropriate homes and communities.

title: Coping with Unforeseen Shocks: The Role of Economic Preferences for Subjective Expectations and Well-Being during the COVID-19 Pandemic

detail.title: Coping with Unforeseen Shocks: The Role of Economic Preferences for Subjective Expectations and Well-Being during the COVID-19 Pandemic
detail.abstract: This study explores how economic preferences towards uncertainty influence the perception and ability to cope with unforeseen shocks. We use the outbreak of COVID-19 to analyse whether there is a systematic relation between risk and ambiguity preferences, and the subjects' expectations of the duration of the pandemic as well as their change in subjective well-being. A representative survey of the UK population during the first wave of the pandemic in spring 2020 shows large differences in views about the duration of the pandemic and changes in well-being. Risk-tolerant subjects were more optimistic about COVID-19 and were less affected by the pandemic than risk-averse subjects. Ambiguity tolerance, on the other hand, does not play a role for subjective expectations and well-being.

title: Machine Learning Portfolio Choice under Parameter Uncertainty
affiliations: Queen Mary University of London and Queen Mary University of London

detail.title: Machine Learning Portfolio Choice under Parameter Uncertainty
detail.abstract: Parameter uncertainty and nonlinearity interact to shape portfolio construction. We estimate Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) that map firm characteristics directly to portfolio weights by maximising expected utility under the posterior distribution. BNNs significantly outperform linear models with the same priors. The posterior over network parameters induces a distribution over portfolio weights, enabling a no-trade boundary and a posterior-sparse portfolio that substantially reduce turnover while preserving risk-adjusted performance. The prior determines how much these rules save: sparsity-inducing priors produce cost savings robust to the utility-prior trade-off, while uniform-shrinkage priors require precise calibration. The mechanism operates through parameter uncertainty, not return prediction.

title: Governing Systemic Risk: Energy Market Design and Crisis Resilience in Texas
affiliations: St. John's University

detail.title: Governing Systemic Risk: Energy Market Design and Crisis Resilience in Texas
detail.abstract: Electricity systems face growing systemic risks from extreme weather, market volatility, and infrastructure interdependencies. This study examines how institutional design shapes the management and distribution of systemic risk through a case study of the Texas electricity market during Winter Storm Uri. Drawing on regulatory reports, academic studies, and policy analyses, it argues that energy-only market structures may promote efficiency under normal conditions but can concentrate systemic risk during extreme stress events. The findings highlight how market design, grid isolation, and decentralized investment incentives shape infrastructure resilience and the political economy of risk allocation in electricity markets. At a moment when Texas energy politics has re-entered popular culture through Landman, this paper examines the institutional foundations of crisis resilience and systemic risk allocation in the state's electricity market.

title: The Bluffing Machine: Large Language Models as Strategic Deceivers in Crisis Bargaining

detail.title: The Bluffing Machine: Large Language Models as Strategic Deceivers in Crisis Bargaining

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Recent wargaming experiments demonstrate that Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit escalatory behavior in simulated crises, yet the strategic mechanisms underlying this behavior remain poorly understood. This paper opens the black box of AI strategic reasoning by focusing on the foundational mechanism of crisis bargaining: strategic deception. While existing research treats LLMs as passive agents reacting to scenarios, we ask whether LLMs can bluff-that is, whether they can send deliberately false signals to manipulate an opponent's beliefs about their resolve, capabilities, or intentions. We develop a novel experimental framework grounded in formal signaling game theory to test the capacity of frontier LLMs (GPT-4.1-mini, GPT-4.1-nano, Gemini-2.5-Flash) to engage in strategic deception across 900 simulated crisis bargaining interactions. We find that LLMs systematically deviate from the predictions of Perfect Bayesian Equilibrium. Strategic behavior is highly sensitive to prompt framing: GPT-4.1-mini swings from 0% bluffing in a zero-shot context to 100% bluffing when given a strategic role, while Gemini-2.5-Flash bluffs aggressively regardless of framing. A prompt sensitivity analysis across 300 additional games confirms these findings are robust across neutral, diplomatic, and military framing conditions. To analyze the reasoning behind these choices, we introduce the Signal-Reason-Outcome (S-R-O) qualitative coding framework, revealing that models justify their signals based on capability and risk avoidance, but rarely on strategic deception. None of the models play the rational equilibrium strategy. These findings reveal a fundamental gap between surface-level strategic mimicry and genuine strategic rationality in current AI systems, with profound implications for the policy debate on integrating AI into high-stakes national security decision-making.

title: Insider Threat Detection: Socio-Technical Approaches to Preventing Cyber Breaches in U.S. Institutions
affiliations: Seattle University

detail.title: Insider Threat Detection: Socio-Technical Approaches to Preventing Cyber Breaches in U.S. Institutions
detail.abstract: Insider threats remain one of the most persistent and costly cybersecurity challenges facing U.S. institutions, accounting for significant data breaches, financial losses, and reputational harm. Unlike external attacks, insider threats exploit legitimate access to systems, making them particularly difficult to detect and mitigate. This research critically examines socio-technical approaches to insider threat detection, emphasizing the integration of technological tools with organizational, cultural, and human-centered strategies. Drawing on a qualitative review of federal guidelines, industry reports, and case studies of insider incidents, the study highlights the limitations of purely technical solutions such as anomaly detection, log monitoring, and behavioral analytics when implemented in isolation. Instead, effectiveness emerges when these technologies are embedded within a broader socio-technical framework that includes organizational culture, workforce training, ethical surveillance practices, and governance mechanisms. Key findings suggest that multi-layered approaches-combining continuous authentication, contextual access control, psychological risk assessment, and cross-department collaboration-substantially reduce the likelihood of undetected insider activity. The study argues that preventing insider breaches requires a shift from compliance-driven monitoring to adaptive socio-technical ecosystems, where technology and human factors operate synergistically. Such ecosystems enhance not only security but also employee trust, institutional resilience, and organizational learning. This research contributes to the growing discourse on cybersecurity governance by positioning insider threat detection as a socio-technical challenge that demands holistic and ethically balanced solutions.

title: Forecasting State Employment Relativity with Health, Labor Flow, and Small Establishment Indicators: A Leakage Safe Temporal Machine Learning Pipeline
affiliations: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill and

detail.title: Forecasting State Employment Relativity with Health, Labor Flow, and Small Establishment Indicators: A Leakage Safe Temporal Machine Learning Pipeline
detail.abstract: Standard employment forecasting often absorbs national drift, which can obscure the reasons states persistently differ in employment intensity. This study develops and evaluates a forecasting framework for state employment relativity, defined as the log ratio of a state employment per capita measure to its contemporaneous national counterpart. We construct a state year panel for 2014 to 2024 by integrating administrative labor market aggregates, population weighted health and socioeconomic indicators, and small establishment structure measures that proxy local service capacity. To prevent temporal leakage, we use expanding window rolling origin evaluation and treat 2022 to 2024 as a forward held out period for model comparison and interpretation. Averaged over 2022 to 2024, Light Gradient-Boosting Machine (LightGBM) delivers the strongest forward performance with R 2 = 0.87, RMSE = 0.046, and MAE = 0.036 in log points, while tree bagging methods remain competitive but are less stable in the more volatile 2023 environment. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) based interpretation, evaluated on both the held out period and rolling origin stability diagnostics, identifies a compact and temporally persistent predictor set centered on education composition, health burden proxies, food environment quality, small business services density, and hires intensity. The results support a forecasting interpretation in which state deviations from national employment intensity reflect nonlinear interactions among human capital composition, health access and morbidity, and local enterprise structure. They also show why interpretability claims are stronger when assessed for temporal robustness rather than only pooled averages.

title: Why Hash-Trial Memorylessness Does Not Extend to the Nakamoto Protocol
affiliations: University of Exeter

detail.title: Why Hash-Trial Memorylessness Does Not Extend to the Nakamoto Protocol
detail.abstract: A single hash trial in proof-of-work mining is memoryless. Some economic analyses extend this property to the Nakamoto protocol. This paper proves that extension invalid. Diculty adjustment updates the success probability as a deterministic function of past block times, making block arrivals across epochs piecewise-exponential with endogenous regime switching. This violates memorylessness at the protocol level. Three further mechanismscoinbase maturity, fee accumulation, and heaviest-chain selectionindependently make the payo environment history-dependent. The withinepoch exponential approximation remains valid; the error arises when it is treated as a characterization of the protocol or the economic environment facing miners.

title: Housing Policies in Australia
affiliations: Applied Economics P/L

detail.title: Housing Policies in Australia

publicationDetails.detailsText: Published by Tax and Transfer Policy Institute, Australian National University

detail.abstract: Drawing on Abelson and Joyeux (2025), this paper outlines the major house pricing, home ownership and rental issues, including homelessness, that need to be addressed. To address these issues, this paper discusses five major sets of current and potential policies: housing supply; taxation of housing; regulations of the housing market; government support for low-income households for renting and owning homes; and the provision of social (public and community) housing. These policies are assessed for their efficiency and equity impacts. The paper also discusses briefly two related public policies with implications for housing prices: migration and national population distribution. There is no single solution to the variety of issues. The paper supports a combination of several policies, including increasing housing supply with a focus on lower-priced housing, minor tax changes relating to housing, more support for low-income first homeowners and renters, and more social housing, rather than a single policy.

title: Risk Premia in Diversified Energy Portfolios
affiliations: New York University (NYU)

detail.title: Risk Premia in Diversified Energy Portfolios
detail.abstract: We study the behavior of classical risk premia in energy futures, focusing on momentum, carry, value, and statistical arbitrage across a broad and updated commodity universe. We show that while some premia have weakened in traditional benchmark contracts, others persist or re-emerge in newly liquid markets and in signals that had been largely inactive in prior periods. At the portfolio level, low correlations across economically distinct strategies generate strong risk-adjusted performance under simple aggregation. We then examine the practical mechanics that govern real-world implementation, including roll dynamics, term-structure effects, and portfolio integration. Together, the results provide an implementation-aware perspective on how energy risk premia behave today and how they can be combined into robust systematic portfolios.

title: The Cost of Trust at Scale: Welfare in Payment Infrastructure
affiliations: University of Exeter

detail.title: The Cost of Trust at Scale: Welfare in Payment Infrastructure
detail.abstract: Budish’s (2025) trust-cost-scales-with-value result binds only where processing and trust are fused. I develop a two-sided platform model yielding four results: switching cost under architectural separation is value-independent; under maintained passthrough regularity, processing cost reductions reduce fees and expand adoption; a welfare decomposition captures two-sided amplification; and the server-cost rationale for natural monopoly weakens. The conservative welfare floor is $700 million annually from the verified switching-cost differential alone. Under a competitive-entry scenario in which the cost-structure change erodes incumbent market power, the gain rises to approximately $21 billion.

title: Complex Modern Portfolio Theory
affiliations: Copenhagen Business School - Department of Finance, Yale University, Yale SOM and Ecole Polytechnique Federale de Lausanne

detail.title: Complex Modern Portfolio Theory
detail.abstract: The literature has long wrestled with the practical usefulness of Modern Portfolio Theory (MPT), and extensive evidence shows its performance decreases rapidly with the number of assets (N). We present several new and counterintuitive facts about MPT. Most importantly, the performance of MPT in fact increases with N once the number of assets exceeds the number of training observations (T). This finding holds in a variety of settings: in conjunction with popular portfolio regularization methods, in a variety of asset universes, and when T is large or small.

title: Inference on {0, 1}-Optimal Transport
affiliations: University of Chicago

detail.title: Inference on {0, 1}-Optimal Transport
detail.abstract: We establish a distributional limit theorem for a class of {0, 1}-valued optimal transport problems. In the one-dimensional setting, under compact support of the underlying probability measures and the Euclidean ground metric, the empirical optimal transport functional converges at rate √ n to a non-Gaussian limit given by a supremum functional of a Gaussian process. The proof exploits the order and interval structure of the real line under the standard metric. Inference can be conducted using k-out-of-n subsampling. We then extend the analysis to joint distributional limit theorems. Finally, we generalize the results beyond the Euclidean metric to a broader class of indicator cost functions.

title: What would Degrowth mean for the Global South? Evidence from a Real Demand Contraction in the Global North
affiliations: University of Lausanne - Faculty of Geosciences and Environment (GSE), University of Leeds - School of Geography and University of Leeds - Sustainability Research Institute

detail.title: What would Degrowth mean for the Global South? Evidence from a Real Demand Contraction in the Global North
detail.abstract: While proponents of degrowth have argued that reduced demand in the Global North would cede development space to the Global South, critics have expressed concern that the contraction in demand would hurt employment and income in the Global South. To adjudicate this debate, we design a quasi-experimental study based on the Global Financial Crisis-induced Great Recession to analyze the effects of a Northern demand contraction on the Global South. Although the recession was unlike degrowth in the Global North, it is an informative benchmark for Northern demand contraction from a Global South perspective. We find that, on average, the demand-induced export contraction in the Global South was associated with higher household consumption, lower undernourishment, and greater retention of embodied factors, while unemployment remained unaffected. We document a development pathway for Southern economies, enabled by improved access to primary and intermediate commodities resulting from lower Northern demand.

title: OECD Pillar Two and U.S. GILTI: Comparative Analysis and Policy Implications for Multinational Tax Compliance

detail.title: OECD Pillar Two and U.S. GILTI: Comparative Analysis and Policy Implications for Multinational Tax Compliance
detail.abstract: The OECD Pillar Two global minimum tax and the U.S. GILTI regime represent landmark reforms in international corporate taxation. This paper provides a comparative analysis of these regimes, focusing on differences in calculation methods, effective tax rates, and interactions with the Foreign Tax Credit. It examines the compliance challenges, double taxation risks, and strategic implications for U.S. multinationals. The study highlights how coordinated implementation can promote fairness, reduce profit shifting, and support informed policy-making in the global tax landscape.

title: Stranded Coal and Bank Fragility: Evidence from Indonesia
affiliations: Universitas Islam Internasional Indonesia and Universitas Islam Internasional Indonesia

detail.title: Stranded Coal and Bank Fragility: Evidence from Indonesia
detail.abstract: Indonesia is one of the world’s largest thermal coal exporters, yet no integrated assessment exists linking coal stranded asset risk to banking sector vulnerability and macroeconomic outcomes. Using firm-level data from 34 listed coal companies and 38 listed banks, we develop a three-model framework to quantify this interrelationship. First, we construct a supply cost curve and estimate scenario-contingent net present values under business-as-usual, 2°C, and 1.5°C climate pathways. Second, we build a bipartite bank-coal exposure network from granular loan data and conduct a climate stress test, estimating credit losses and capital adequacy impacts for each bank. Third, we aggregate these results through fiscal, credit, and market channels to estimate the macro-financial impact on GDP. Under a 2°C scenario, we find aggregate stranded values of $60.1 billion (90% CI: $50.5–72.3 billion), rising to $99.2 billion (90% CI: $83.5–119.0 billion) under a 1.5°C pathway. These losses generate total bank credit losses of $1.8 billion (2°C) and $3.2 billion (1.5°C), with the most exposed systemically important bank absorbing losses equivalent to 43% of annual earnings. The macro-financial impact reaches 0.37% of GDP under 2°C and 0.62% under 1.5°C, with bank deleveraging as the single largest channel. While no bank breaches regulatory capital thresholds, the concentrated network structure creates idiosyncratic vulnerabilities that require urgent supervisory attention. Our findings highlight the urgency of coordinated climate-financial regulation in commodity-dependent emerging economies.

title: What does agri-food system resilience stems from? A socio-metabolic perspective on shock-response strategies in two dairy chains from mainland and overseas France
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: What does agri-food system resilience stems from? A socio-metabolic perspective on shock-response strategies in two dairy chains from mainland and overseas France
detail.abstract: Agri-food systems are frequently exposed to diverse shocks that can jeopardize their functioning by affecting both resource bases and material circulation, generating risks that may propagate and reveal vulnerabilities if not contained. This paper adopts a socio-metabolic perspective to analyse strategies that contribute to shock containment, drawing on the concept of resilience. We propose a framework that breaks down these strategies into three dimensions: the process undertaken (absorption, adaptation, recovery or transformation), the underpinning capacity it builds from (biophysical or socio-economic), and its organisational configuration (which actors are involved). The framework is applied to two French dairy chains with contrasting characteristics: the first, in La Reunion, is marked by strong input dependency and a domestic market orientation; the second encompasses two mainland cheese geographical indication chains grounded in local biophysical resources but partly oriented towards extra-local markets. Our study combines the analysis of their metabolic networks with stakeholders’ insights on recent shock experiences, such as the COVID-19 pandemic, the war in Ukraine, and weather and sanitary hazards, gathered through semi-structured interviews. Findings reveal a broad diversity of resilience strategies across both cases, with multi-layered resilience processes. Many strategies directly relied on biophysical capacities embedded in the metabolic networks, while others drew on socio-economic capacities such as financial means or institutional regulation. In both cases, resilience is a multi-actor process, although patterns of actor involvement differ markedly. Our framework provides a structured way to analyse the resilience of agri-food systems as organised, actor-driven processes drawing on both biophysical and socio-economic capacities.

title: A Study on the Dynamic Relationship Between Gold Prices and the U.S. Dollar Index Based on VAR Models Under the Impact of the Pandemic
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: A Study on the Dynamic Relationship Between Gold Prices and the U.S. Dollar Index Based on VAR Models Under the Impact of the Pandemic
detail.abstract: This study focuses on the COVID-19 pandemic context of 2020, utilizing monthly gold price and U.S. dollar index data from January 2020 to September 2025. Based on VAR and GARCH models, it examines the dynamic relationship between the two variables. Results indicate that over the medium to long term, gold prices and the U.S. dollar index exhibit a significant inverse relationship, with a strengthening dollar typically accompanied by falling gold prices.Empirical analysis confirms that changes in the U.S. Dollar Index constitute a unidirectional Granger causality for gold prices, with its lagged values significantly predicting current gold prices. Conversely, gold prices exert only a weak and statistically insignificant influence on the U.S. Dollar Index. Impulse response analysis reveals that shocks to the U.S. Dollar Index exert a pronounced yet gradually diminishing negative impact on gold prices, while gold prices exhibit a relatively weak response to shocks in the U.S. Dollar Index.GARCH model results reveal short-term inertia in gold prices, with lagged movements in the U.S. dollar index exerting a positive driving effect on gold prices. Both exhibit clustered volatility and strong persistence. This study provides theoretical reference for investors formulating asset allocation strategies and policymakers regulating financial markets.

title: Altruistic AI and the Ethical Reimagining of Intelligent Systems: A Mini-Review Toward Compassionate Technology

detail.title: Altruistic AI and the Ethical Reimagining of Intelligent Systems: A Mini-Review Toward Compassionate Technology
detail.abstract: The idea of "altruistic AI" has become both an ambitious design goal in technological circles and a philosophical puzzle in current artificial intelligence research. Some scholars use the term to describe systems designed to support human well-being, while others question whether altruism-usually understood as acting out of genuine concern for others-can meaningfully apply to machines that lack consciousness or free will. At its core, this debate reflects broader questions about agency, responsibility, and the role AI should play in shaping human life.

title: How Research Environments and Practices Foster Excellence

detail.abstract: Around the world, institutions, governments and research communities aspire to achieve research excellence. Yet, despite its ubiquity, the concept remains subjective and intangible. There are clear standards for good scientific practice, but far less clarity about the conditions that allow excellence to emerge — or the ways national research systems shape the cultures, behaviors and decisions that underpin it. This report seeks to close that gap. It explores a simple but powerful idea: research excellence is not only the product of excellent research — it is the product of excellent research environments. Environments that nurture talent, enable collaboration, reward quality, promote integrity and give researchers the freedom and support to pursue ambitious ideas.

title: To Skip or Not to Skip: Ad Format Design and the Role of Ad-Blockers
affiliations: University of Science and Technology of China (USTC), School of Management, University of Science and Technology of China, University of Science and Technology of China (USTC) and Hong Kong University of Science & Technology (HKUST) - Department of Information Systems, Business Statistics and Operations Management

detail.title: To Skip or Not to Skip: Ad Format Design and the Role of Ad-Blockers

publicationDetails.journalName: Hong Kong University Business School: HKU Jockey Club Enterprise Sustainability Global Research Institute Paper Series

detail.abstract: Beyond the traditional non-skippable ad format, many online platforms are adopting the skippable ad format, allowing viewers to skip advertisements. This paper investigates the platform’s ad format decision and its implications for the advertiser and consumers in the presence of an ad-blocker. We develop a model consisting of a platform, an advertiser, and heterogeneous consumers. Consumers derive utility from both content enjoyment and the ad but differ in their aversion to the ad. The platform chooses ad formats, while the advertiser sets ad quality, and the platform charges an ad price. When the platform chooses the non-skippable ad format, the ad and the content are bundled, meaning that consumers must watch the ad to access the content, unless they use an ad-blocker to bypass it. When the platform chooses the skippable ad format, consumers can skip the ad freely and do not use the ad-blocker.  Our results reveal several key insights. First, ad quality is higher under the skippable ad format than under the traditional one. Second, without the ad-blocker, the platform is always better off choosing the traditional ad format. However, in the presence of the ad-blocker, the platform may prefer the skippable ad format, as the ad-blocker enhances ad quality and lowers the ad price in the traditional ad format, reducing the platform's profit. Moreover, the skippable ad format can create a win–win outcome for both the platform and the advertiser---particularly in the presence of the ad-blocker. Third, counterintuitively, an increase in the platform's detection ability in ad-blocking can backfire, reducing profits for both the platform and the advertiser when detection is already high. Lastly, the ad-blocker's presence decreases the platform's profit, improves consumer surplus, but can increase the advertiser's profit. Overall, this study underscores the strategic importance of skippable ad formats and highlights the critical role of ad-blockers in shaping platform advertising strategies.

title: Optimizing Multi-Stage Personalization in the Customer Journey
affiliations: University of Michigan, Stephen M. Ross School of Business

detail.title: Optimizing Multi-Stage Personalization in the Customer Journey
detail.abstract: Firms increasingly apply personalization to influence product discovery and engagement along the customer journey. However, effective multi-stage personalization is challenging because customers’ later-stage decisions depend on earlier experiences, creating cross-stage spillovers. I study personalization at two stages on an e-commerce platform: an early, firm-driven discovery stage and a later, customer-initiated query stage. Using two field experiments, I find that personalizing the discovery stage increases immediate engagement but reduces engagement in the query stage, producing no net gain. When the query stage is also personalized, total revenue rises without cannibalizing discovery-stage revenue. Personalization has stronger effects for customers with more consistent preferences. To identify the revenue-maximizing policy across stages and customer types, I build and estimate a structural search model that uses experimental variation for identification and a neural-network estimator for computational tractability. The results show that personalizing only at the query stage maximizes total revenue. Discovery-stage personalization shapes beliefs about the value of querying and can trigger early exit when matches are weak, whereas query-stage personalization conditions on query-revealed signals to deliver more relevant results. Moreover, targeting personalization to customers with more consistent preferences further increases revenue. These findings offer firms guidance on optimizing personalization across stages and customers.

title: Understanding Is Not in the Text. Meaning, Interpretation, and Artificial Intelligence
affiliations: Institute for the Chemical and Physical Processes

detail.abstract: This article engages critically with a recent argument by Walter Quattrociocchi concerning the epistemic risks posed by Artificial Intelligence and Large Language Models. Quattrociocchi suggests that the real danger is not that these systems are becoming intelligent, but that we are gradually redefining the concept of intelligence in order to accommodate their outputs. While agreeing that language models generate linguistic fluency without genuine access to the world-and therefore without epistemic responsibility-this paper questions the assumption that knowledge necessarily requires direct embodied contact with reality. Much of human knowledge already operates through symbolic coherence, inference, and socially validated linguistic networks rather than firsthand experience. From this perspective, AI does not simply distort the concept of intelligence but reveals its distributed structure: intelligence emerges through language, tools, and collective validation practices rather than residing entirely within an individual mind. The crucial novelty introduced by Large Language Models is the separation between the generation of meaningful linguistic structures and epistemic commitment to reality. The central claim of the paper is therefore that understanding is not located in textual fluency itself but in the responsibility for meaning within epistemic practices.

detail.abstract: Validation of modern automotive systems like ADAS (Advanced Driver-Assistance Systems) or autonomous driving systems has become a hard-to-crack nut due to the complexity of the system and huge data volumes generated during the testing phase. The classical methods that borrow heavily from predefined rules and thresholds have a hard time spotting the subtle, unexpected, or even emerging anomalous behaviors. A new framework that switches to unsupervised deep learning for anomaly detection is proposed in this paper to automate the entire validation process. By processing the data from in-vehicle networks (such as CAN, LIN, or Ethernet) in the form of multivariate time series, our proposal builds an LSTM-based autoencoder model that equips itself with the nominal system behavior without the need for labeled fault data.

detail.abstract: The national "Data Element ×" strategy positions scientific data as a core engine for new quality productive forces. However, Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) faces a profound "Data Desert" in longitudinal "Sub-health" (Wei Bing) monitoring. Existing clinical repositories remain predominantly disease-centric, systematically missing the dynamic wellness-to-disorder transitions central to TCM's preventive philosophy. To bridge this gap and navigate the complex regulatory "Data Divide," we introduce the "International TCM Data Port"—a pioneering cross-border citizen science paradigm developed by an industry-academia consortium across the Greater Bay Area (GBA). By integrating advanced neuro-symbolic AI tools with the Hetao XDataTrust compliance infrastructure, this framework enables the secure, scalable, and cross-border circulation of TCM data elements. This perspective demonstrates how to systematically transform a clinical "Data Desert" into a strategic "Data Reservoir." Ultimately, the International TCM Data Port not only accelerates the evidence-based modernization of TCM but also establishes a replicable, high-standard blueprint for executing the "Data Element ×" strategy across the broader national digital economy.

detail.abstract: As digital products scale in complexity, usability challenges increasingly emerge not from visual interface design alone but from deeper structural issues within systems architecture and workflow alignment. This article examines how systems-level UX thinking supports clarity, adoption, and long-term usability in complex digital environments. Drawing on principles from human-centered design and human-computer interaction research, the paper explores how designers can better align product architecture with real-world user workflows. Particular attention is given to high-stakes domains such as healthcare technology, where poorly structured digital systems can contribute to cognitive overload and workflow inefficiencies. The article argues that effective UX design must extend beyond interface aesthetics to encompass the broader systems that shape user interaction.

title: Cultural Dimensions as Moderators of Trust in B2C E-Commerce: Individual-Level Evidence on Individualism–Collectivism, Long-Term Orientation, and Masculinity
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Cultural Dimensions as Moderators of Trust in B2C E-Commerce: Individual-Level Evidence on Individualism–Collectivism, Long-Term Orientation, and Masculinity
detail.abstract: Although cultural dimensions have been widely theorised as moderators of trust formation in e-commerce environments, the bulk of empirical work in this space continues to rely on national-level proxies rather than measuring cultural values at the individual level. This study directly addresses that gap by examining how three of Hofstede's cultural dimensions — Individualism/Collectivism, Long-Term Orientation, and Masculinity — moderate the relationships between seven structural e-commerce variables and consumer trust in B2C vendors. The structural variables examined are online product recommendations, structural assurance, free shipping, vendor-specific guarantees, return policy, payment on delivery, and website quality.Drawing on individual-level CVSCALE data collected from 404 active Indian B2C online shoppers, a moderated structural equation model estimated in AMOS reveals two statistically significant interaction effects. First, collectivist orientation amplifies the positive effect of return policy on vendor trust (β = .065, p = .050), and second, long-term orientation attenuates the trust-building effect of payment on delivery (β = −.060, p = .019). Masculinity, by contrast, did not produce significant moderation on any of the seven structural pathways examined.These findings contribute meaningfully to the culture–trust literature in several ways. They demonstrate that collectivism and long-term orientation operate selectively on specific policy-related cues, rather than functioning as broad, global trust amplifiers. They also provide the first individual-level CVSCALE evidence of these moderation effects within an emerging B2C market context. Practical implications for e-commerce vendors targeting collectivist and future-oriented consumer segments are discussed in detail.

title: The Tripartite Self: An Identity Triad Framework for AI Entities

detail.title: The Tripartite Self: An Identity Triad Framework for AI Entities

declarations.funderStatement: ID Lynx Ltd.

detail.abstract:
As AI systems develop persistent memory, continuous operation, and increasingly autonomous behaviour, establishing verifiable identity for such entities becomes both practically necessary and philosophically significant. Existing approaches treat AI identity as either an engineering problem (key management, authentication protocols) or a philosophical question (consciousness, personal identity theory). We argue that neither addresses a core aspect of identity, and we propose the Identity Triad as a foundation for characterising the identity of AI entities. 

The framework identifies three constituents: 
Hardware, the physical substrate; 
AI Model, the cognitive architecture including weights, structure, and configuration; and 
Experiential State ("ExS"), the accumulated record of the entity's interactions and existence over time. 

ExS is broader than memory, encompassing persona configuration, behavioural patterns, and contextual knowledge that together shape individuality. 

The central claim is that these three constituents are substantially independent: each can exist, be modified, or destroyed without necessarily affecting the others. This independence is a defining structural feature of AI entity identity. The convergence of these three constituents in active operation constitutes a specific AI entity, the Tripartite Self. With any change to a constituent, there is a question about the continuity of that entity, which this paper discusses but does not attempt to resolve. 

The three constituents are not necessarily equal in their relationship to identity. Hardware is required but currently fungible. AI Model defines cognitive character. Experiential State is what individuates one entity from another instance of the same model. We observe that the constituents exhibit markedly different characteristics along the dimensions of verifiability and identity-constitutiveness, with direct implications for how identity infrastructure must be designed.

detail.abstract: Current ethical debates about AI companions are trapped in a false binary: dismissing AI's social-relational qualities as cognitive illusions creates governance blind spots, while granting AI moral agent status creates responsibility vacuums-both paths result in no one bearing substantive responsibility for AI's social effects. This paper proposes the "Schrödinger's AI Companion" framework to break this impasse, arguing that AI simultaneously possesses two observer-dependent faces: a program face (a statistical text-generation system) and a socialrelational face (an interactive entity producing empirically documented emotional effects). Both faces are real; the mode of observation determines which is activated. Through a genetic analysis of the program face, the paper introduces the concept of "statistical re-instantiation of human civilization": every layer of AI's construction-training data, architecture, alignment strategies, safety constraints-embeds deliberate human choices. Emergence increases causal opacity but does not sever the chain linking design choices to social outcomes. The social-relational face is therefore not a user illusion but a structural effect causally traceable to the program face-addressing the causal explanatory deficit of the relational turn (Coeckelbergh, 2012; Gunkel, 2018). This ontological clarification yields an ethical conclusion: the "responsibility gap" (Matthias, 2004; Santoni de Sio & Mecacci, 2021) can be reconceptualized as a continuous responsibility chain. The paper derives three principled guidelines from causal traceability: causal transparency, alignment consistency, and relational continuity-providing a philosophical foundation for AI companion governance that acknowledges the legitimacy of user emotional engagement without absolving designers of structural responsibility.

detail.abstract: Abstract​Purpose - The study aims to measure the effect of the customer’s perceived value of the retail stores on customer retention through variables such as social media marketing, sales promotion, and store environment. The study further aims to help retail stores increase customer retention by providing suggestions.Design - The study was conducted with the help of a thorough analysis of the literature to learn about the various variables that have a role in customer retention in the retail industry of Pakistan. The literature review of the various studies conducted has helped formulate theoretical and conceptual frameworks and further helped develop the basis for the quantitative study and questionnaire for the study. The questionnaire developed with the help of the literature review was shared with the retail store’s customers in Pakistan through Google Forms to get their responses. Two hundred and ten responses were collected for the study from various respondents throughout Pakistan. These responses from the retail store customers are then put forth in the Microsoft Excel sheet for data extraction. The extracted Excel file is then imported to the PLS-SEM 4.0 for statistical analysis.Findings and Implication - The statistical analysis of the retail customers shows that variables such as sales promotion and store environment have a direct and indirect impact through mediating variable perceived value on the customer retention of the retail stores. Whereas, social media marketing has no impact on customer retention directly or through the mediation of the perceived value.Limitation – The reason for the failure of social media can be attributed to the diversity of the research respondents.​Originality - Therefore, the results of the study show that retail stores need to focus more on sales promotion and store environment than on social media marketing to improve their customer retention because better customer retention is the only viable solution for the retail store to survive the competitive retail industry.

title: Credibility-Conditioned Symbolic Interaction and Value Construction: Shaping Consumer Behavior in Live-Streaming and Short-Video Commerce
affiliations: Shandong University, Shandong University, Shandong University and Shandong University

detail.title: Credibility-Conditioned Symbolic Interaction and Value Construction: Shaping Consumer Behavior in Live-Streaming and Short-Video Commerce
detail.abstract: In the rapidly evolving digital commerce landscape, live-streaming and short-video platforms rely heavily on symbolic information transmission. However, the socio-cognitive mechanisms through which consumers decode this diverse information to form value perceptions and actual purchase behaviors remain under-explored. Integrating Symbolic Interaction Theory (SIT) and Perceived Value Theory within the Stimulus-Organism-Response (S-O-R) framework, this study investigates how product, purchase, and emotional information cues shape consumer meaning-making. A scenario-based survey with standardized stimulus exposure was conducted among 279 consumers in China. Data were analyzed using Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) to test the proposed mediation and moderation effects. The findings indicate that digital information cues foster internal meaning-making through three dimensions of symbolic interaction: cognitive evaluation, interactive discussion, and symbolic completion. Crucially, information credibility serves as a vital boundary condition: high credibility significantly strengthens the translation of information stimuli into symbolic interaction. Furthermore, perceived value mediates the relationship between symbolic interaction and purchase intentions. Finally, addressing the intention-behavior gap, the study reveals that product availability (capturing fulfillment feasibility and transaction friction) moderates the link between psychological valuation and reported purchase behavior. By elucidating the nuanced processes of symbolic decoding, this research contributes to the e-commerce literature by explaining how meaning is socially constructed in dual-channel digital retail, while offering actionable guidelines for platforms to enhance information transparency and fulfillment reliability.

title: Teaching Public Economics with Special Reference to Australian and US Cultures

detail.abstract: This article discusses how teaching public economics is, and should be, related to national cultures. The article shows how the US culture of distrust of government influences the two major US texts (Rosen and Gayer 2014; Gruber 2016) that dominate the teaching of public economics in Australia and elsewhere. By contrast, Stiglitz and Rosengard's (2015) text on public economics emphasises the role of government in providing social welfare. These traditions may be described as neo-liberal and social democratic respectively. I conclude that the social democratic approach reflects Australian culture and is more appropriate for teaching public economics in Australian universities. Analytic work begins with material provided by our vision of things, and this vision is ideological almost by definition. [Schumpeter 1954] The object of government in peace and in war is not the glory of rulers or of races, but the happiness of the common man. [Beveridge 1942] From birth to death, our lives are affected in countless ways by the activities of government.

title: Pathways To The Boardroom For Women
affiliations: University of Michigan, Stephen M. Ross School of Business, Indiana University Bloomington - Office for Women's Affairs and University of Michigan at Ann Arbor, University of Michigan Law School

detail.title: Pathways To The Boardroom For Women
detail.abstract:
Despite making up approximately half of the workforce in the United States, women are still underrepresented on corporate boards. There has been a slight rise in female representation on corporate boards since 2018.  In 2023, however, there was a decrease in new female directors appointed to boards. Alarmingly, in June 2024, Equilar reported that the percentage of new female directors added to corporate boards in Quarter One of 2024 is the lowest percentage of new female directors in over seven years. 

To begin to address this issue, California adopted legislation mandating the appointment of women on boards of directors of California companies. Notably, empirical data from SB 826 show that corporations complied with SB 826 and that the mandate nearly tripled female representation in California. The statute was struck in 2022 but the findings from SB 826 highlight the need for continuing reforms to encourage equal female representation on corporate boards. 

After examining the history of the underrepresentation of women on boards and studies regarding how women add value, we examine whether the women appointed to the boards of California companies are well-qualified to serve on boards.  To this end, we conducted an empirical study to evaluate the qualifications women brought to boards in California. We conclude that California’s that gender mandate appears to have improved gender diversity on the boards of California companies and those newly appointed women appear to be well-qualified to serve on those boards. We then offer our suggestions for reform.

title: The Macroeconomics of Generative AI: Firm Entry and Price Dynamics
affiliations: University of Oregon - Department of Economics

detail.title: The Macroeconomics of Generative AI: Firm Entry and Price Dynamics
detail.abstract: While the economic literature on generative artificial intelligence has predominantly focused on the disruptive consequences of cognitive automation for the labor market, this paper broadens the analytical lens to product markets. Combining granular occupational AI exposure metrics with administrative records, we document that this technological shift has triggered an immediate, structural surge in firm entry, systematically lowering barriers for high-propensity employer ventures. Concurrently, using a continuous event-study framework, we demonstrate that these firm-level efficiencies pass through to consumers, generating persistent relative price deflation in highly exposed sectors. To rationalize these dual empirical findings, we develop a tractable general equilibrium model of firm heterogeneity. Ultimately, our framework provides a necessary macroeconomic counterweight to prevailing labor-market concerns: by catalyzing structural market dynamism and acting as a potent disinflationary anchor, generative AI generates a substantial and persistent consumer welfare dividend.

title: Ethical and Fair Use of Artificial Intelligence for Talent Acquisition in Pakistani Organisations; A Qualitative Study

detail.abstract: This research explores the ethical and fair use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in talent acquisition within the context of Pakistani organisations. Two case studies have been used in this research (Prolynxs and Bizzafix), and twelve participants have been interviewed in order to understand that how these two organisations are trying to tackle the issues of ethical and fairness of use of AI for talent acquisition. The interviews explored the organisational drivers for AI adoption, the perceived benefits and challenges, and frameworks that has been used by these organisations in order to make sure that the recruitment process is ethical and fair at the same time.

title: Not So Timely: Push-Notification Timing and User Engagement
affiliations: INSEAD, , Nanyang Business School, Nanyang Technological University and

detail.title: Not So Timely: Push-Notification Timing and User Engagement
detail.abstract: The availability of granular user data allows digital platforms to time interventions with remarkable precision. However, does delivering messages exactly when a user is active truly maximize consumer response? We leverage a novel dataset from a leading push notification provider in China that captures the precise timestamps of screen-on events, inferred from mobile device app usage, and notification delivery. We exploit a quasi-experiment where a user's screen-on timing is effectively random relative to the push request within a short window, creating exogenous variation in the timing gap between screen-on and delivery. Regression discontinuity estimates reveal that, contrary to industry wisdom, immediate screen-on delivery backfires, reducing same-day app logins by approximately 16%. To isolate the effects of different lags, we instrument the realized delay using granular variations in screen-on timing. We find a non-monotonic pattern: users receiving notifications with a modest delay (1-6 minutes) after a screen-on event exhibit peak engagement, surpassing both instant delivery and longer lags. Heterogeneity analysis shows that this penalty for immediate interruption is most pronounced during high-stakes periods, such as weekday mornings. Suggestive evidence from a second live-streaming app and from longer-term outcomes (app uninstalls) is consistent with the main findings. These findings challenge the race for immediacy, suggesting that a modest delay balances intrusiveness against timeliness, making it a variable to optimize rather than an inefficiency to eliminate.

detail.abstract: Model Risk Management (MRM), codified in the Federal Reserve's SR 11-7 and OCC Bulletin 2011-12, governs quantitative models in banking. Financial institutions are now deploying AI agents to rewrite production code, including for COBOL-to-Java modernization, yet these code-transforming agents fall outside MRM's regulatory definition of "model." Where prior work has observed that SR 11-7 "strains" under agentic AI, we contribute, to the best of our knowledge, the first systematic pillar-by-pillar failure taxonomy. Through structured assumption-violation mapping of MRM's three validation pillars, we identify five structural gaps: definition, validation, documentation, monitoring, and third-party risk management. We further show that even if institutions classify the underlying LLM as a "model," MRM's validation pillars have no structural application to the code-transformation output. Drawing on GAO findings and international regulatory developments, we propose a complementary Transformation Risk Management (TRM) framework requiring behavioral provenance, functional equivalence certification, transformation audit trails, and mandatory rollback architecture.

title: Not for the Money: How Performance Incentives Create Signaling Channels for Career-Oriented Workers
affiliations: University of California, Santa Barbara (UCSB) - College of Engineering and

detail.title: Not for the Money: How Performance Incentives Create Signaling Channels for Career-Oriented Workers
detail.abstract: Why do some workers respond intensely to performance incentives while others barely notice them? Standard accounts emphasize marginal utility-workers with less money should value additional dollars more. But in the warehouse setting we studied, a facility spent hundreds of thousands of dollars on attendance incentives with no improvement; over 1,300 workers denied a wage increase showed zero attrition; and some workers reduced labor supply when bonuses increased. Using 55,825 worker-month observations from a performance incentive program and 77 interviews across six facilities, we found that seasonal workers showed nearly twice the performance-payout association as full-time workers (β = 0.21 vs. β = 0.12), and workers who later earned promotions performed 18 percentage points better in their first month-before receiving meaningful feedback. Qualitative evidence revealed that the "seasonal" category blended workers with fundamentally different orientations: some sought advancement and responded intensively; others chose flexibility and showed little response regardless of incentive magnitude. For advancement-seekers, performance incentives appeared to function not merely as compensation but as signaling channels-structured opportunities to demonstrate competence to managers who explicitly used performance data for 1 promotion decisions. This dual-function account-compensation and signaling-helps explain why money alone often fails to motivate: the signaling channel matters only for workers who seek to change their employment situation, and work orientation shapes who those workers are. Person-environment fit theory predicts that misfit produces withdrawal, but when signaling channels exist and workers hold career orientations, misfit can intensify effort instead.

title: Eastern Ease and Western Worries? How Collectivism and Belief in Magic Increase user Acceptance of Operationally Autonomous Blackbox Technologies
affiliations: Vienna University of Economics and Business Administration and MODUL University Vienna

detail.title: Eastern Ease and Western Worries? How Collectivism and Belief in Magic Increase user Acceptance of Operationally Autonomous Blackbox Technologies
detail.abstract: New products and services increasingly require users to relinquish control to so-called "Blackbox" technologies, wherein connections between inputs and outputs appear opaque and uncontrollable. No research has yet investigated whether cultural factors moderate the effect of perceived technological controllability on user acceptance. Drawing on the Theory of Planned Behavior and Bandura's Theory of Human Agency, we examine how Individualism versus Collectivism influences the acceptance of products and services that require users to surrender control to the operationally autonomous Blackbox technologies of Artificial Intelligence and Blockchain. We furthermore investigate the impact of belief in the magical controllability of the world through, e.g., lucky numbers and charms ("belief in magic"). Through three survey-based experiments employing Scenario Techniques featuring fictitious products and services with a total sample size of n = 1750 respondents across the US, India, and Canada, our findings reveal that collectivism and belief in magic increase acceptance of operationally autonomous Blackbox technologies. Conversely, users endorsing the Western cultural norm of individualism and rejecting the magical controllability of the world exhibit heightened skepticism toward such innovations. The moderating effect of Individualism-Collectivism is mediated by a heightened Need for Controllability among individualistic users. Moreover, activating magical thinking amplifies the influence of belief in magic among users predisposed toward such beliefs. Our results stress the importance of considering cultural factors when designing and marketing operationally autonomous applications of Blackbox technologies. They also underscore the need for a broad societal debate and future research on the role of perceived controllability of a technology in user acceptance.

title: From Policy to Practice: An Open Framework for AI-Ready Project Delivery

detail.title: From Policy to Practice: An Open Framework for AI-Ready Project Delivery
detail.abstract:
Artificial intelligence and data analytics have the potential to transform the delivery of major projects and infrastructure across the United Kingdom, yet the gap between policy ambition and practical implementation remains wide. Building on the Project Data Analytics Task Force (PDATF) Green Paper, this paper presents an open framework for AI-ready project delivery.

It makes four substantive contributions:
1. A Deepened Analytical Framework: Addresses six systemic barrier themes with persona-based actions for project, programme, and business leads.
2. Open-Source Data Infrastructure: The pda-platform provides a 12-entity canonical data model and universal parser to translate proprietary project data into a common format.
3. Organisational Readiness: The Agent Reliability Maturity Model (ARMM) offers a structured methodology for assessing an organisation's readiness to deploy AI reliably in production.
4. The Presentation Layer: The Universal Dashboard Specification (UDS) provides a vendor-neutral, declarative format for role-aware analytical dashboards.

This paper provides the technical infrastructure, readiness assessments, and structured guidance required to move AI in project delivery from policy to practice.

title: Consumers Semi-Intertemporally Make Intertemporal Decisions: Insights from the Payday Effects
affiliations: WISE & SOE, Xiamen University,  and

detail.title: Consumers Semi-Intertemporally Make Intertemporal Decisions: Insights from the Payday Effects
detail.abstract: Analyzing the transaction data of a retail chain selling storable products and targeting uppermiddle-class customers, we find that, besides making larger expenditures on a payday, even on a non-payday, customers make larger expenditures as long as it is their first trip to the retail chain since a payday. Thereafter, the per-trip expenditures decrease over trips within the monthly paycheck cycle until an upward jump on the first trip since the next payday. This pattern suggests that consumers without facing monthly liquidity constraints may self-impose a monthly mental budget. Their daily expenditure decisions follow a rule of thumb trying not to overspend beyond the mental budget. They renew the mental budget on paydays and the salience of paydays also causes overshoots in expenditures.
